- Army aviation. 

- Signals intelligence (SIGINT) enablers. 

- Measurement and signature intelligence enablers. 

- Military working dog teams. 

- Biometrics collection. 

- Tactical PSYOP teams. 

- CA teams. 

5-95. The cordon and search force (for example, a company) often receives additional assets to assist in a cordon and search operation based on availability and the METT-TC (I) variables. Assets may serve as teams in the security or search (or assault) element, or they may remain independent and on call. Assets may be internal or external to the tasked battalion or company and include military police, engineers, CA, PSYOP, military intelligence, or artillery who form any of the following: 

- Mine detection teams. 

- Demolition teams. 

- Interrogation teams. 

- Documentation or biometric teams (use a recorder with a camera). 

- Scout dog teams. 

- Fire support teams. 

- Tactical air control parties. 

- CA teams. 

- Detainee and enemy prisoner of war (EPW) teams. 

- Tunnel reconnaissance teams. 

- Crowd control teams. 

- Female search teams. 

- Escort parties. 

- Transportation teams. 

###### **Command Element** 

5-96. The command element (battalion main CP and, when established, a battalion tactical CP) serves as the headquarters of the cordon and search force. The battalion commander applies the same planning and decision-making techniques as those applied in other operations. While sudden opportunities may arise with little planning time, the nature of a search and what it may uncover can result in significant amounts of time spent in the objective area. The commander remains prepared to execute cordon and search operations with very little notice and to spend many hours, even days, conducting the operation. 

5-97. The command element considers numerous mission variables when planning and preparing for a cordon and search operation. The commander identifies elements and assigns units to them, along with a clear task and purpose. Ideally, existing base units (platoons and squads) within the rifle company are task-organized into a security element, a search (or assault) element, and support elements for the operation. These elements organize necessary sub-elements for accomplishing the mission. Their command element (company primary CP and, when established, a company alternate CP) normally nests within one other element rather than travel as its own entity. 

###### **Security Element** 

5-98. The security element is responsible for sealing off the objective by emplacing outer and inner cordons. It limits or prevents enemy and civilian influence in the objective area and prevents targets from escaping the cordon. It may receive the bulk of the available combat power due to multiple avenues of approach and a requirement to disperse widely across the objective area in accomplishing its mission. It may have to establish multiple blocking positions and observation posts and conduct patrols to seal off the target area. Whether the cordon and search force travels as a single force (through a single ingress point) or moves in multiple elements on multiple routes (multidirectional ingress), the security element normally leads movement. It must have the inner and outer cordons in place, or nearly in place, prior to actions by other elements. 

5-99. As security elements deploy to establish outer and inner cordons, the actions of both reinforce each other, creating an environment that prevents unwanted influences and actions—from both outside the objective area and inside the target area—from interfering with mission success. Cordon elements (outer and inner) focus both inward and outward for security purposes. The cordon requirements, the security element’s method for movement into the objective area, and its chosen manner for occupying the positions that compose both cordons dictate its actions during deployment. The security element leader employs information collection assets, internal and external to the battalion and its companies, to observe the target area before the approach of the security elements. Cordon establishment starts when the first security element reaches its release point position or similar control measure, and it ends as the security element seals off the objective area.

5-100. The establishment of the outer cordon (see figure 5-3) during the cordon phase requires detailed planning and coordination and meticulous integration and synchronization to achieve the required effects. The outer cordon prevents anyone from entering the objective area and assists the inner cordon in preventing the enemy (insurgency) from escaping the objective area. The element leader of the outer cordon maintains situational awareness and, within the commander’s abilities, situational understanding to facilitate the progress of the operation, specifically the inner cordon and search efforts. Tactical tasks associated with the outer cordon security element include those following: 

- _Block_ —a tactical mission task that denies the enemy access to an area or an avenue of approach (FM 3-90). (The definition of this term is different when the term is referring to an obstacle effect.) 

- _Deny_ —a task to hinder or prevent the enemy from using terrain, space, personnel, supplies, or facilities (ATP 3-21.20). 

- _Interdict_ —a tactical mission task in which a unit prevents, disrupts, or delays the enemy’s use of an area or route in any domain (FM 3-90). 

**Figure 5-3. Cordon and search (inner and outer cordons)** 5-101. Establishment of the inner cordon requires the same level of planning, coordination, integration, and synchronization as the outer cordon to achieve the desired results. The inner cordon seals off the target area to protect the search (or assault) element from enemy activity. It prevents enemy movement in the target area and prevents enemy entry or departure. The security element is properly armed and equipped to control the ground and mitigate the most likely issues they are to face, as determined during planning and preparation in the reconnaissance phase (see paragraph 5-43 for information on the reconnaissance phase). Tactical tasks associated with the inner cordon security element include those following:

- _Contain_ —a tactical mission task in which a unit stops, holds, or surrounds an enemy force (FM 3-90). 

- _Fix_ —a tactical mission task in which a unit prevents the enemy from moving from a specific location for a specific period (FM 3-90). (The definition of this term is different when used as an obstacle effect.) 

- _Overwatch_ —a task that positions an element to support the movement of another element with immediate fire (ATP 3-21.10). 

- _Suppress_ —a tactical mission task in which a unit temporarily degrades a force or weapon system from accomplishing its mission (FM 3-90). 

5-102. During the search (actions on the objective) phase, the security element maintains the inner and outer cordons. The inner cordon overwatches the actions on the objective, prevents egress from the target area, and coordinates actions with the outer cordon. The outer cordon prevents external influences from entering the objective area, prevents or controls movement into and out of the objective area, and coordinates with the inner cordon. 

5-103. Whether the cordon and search force uses a single egress point or executes a multidirectional egress, the security element is normally the last to depart. The inner and outer cordons and their controls on the objective and target areas provide overwatch for the search (or assault) and support elements. Should the withdrawal be cancelled by design or by enemy action, the cordon remains in place. Once the other cordon and search force elements have committed to the withdrawal and are safely away from the target area, the security element first collapses the inner and then the outer cordon. 

###### **Search (or Assault) Element** 

5-104. The search (or assault) element’s mission is to clear, search, and conduct site exploitation on the objective and thereby to locate and seize contraband material and to identify, search, or detain suspected insurgents. The search (or assault) element moves as either the second or third element of movement in the order of march. When resistance is not expected or when speed and surprise are paramount, the commander places the search (or assault) element as the second march element, so it can move immediately and directly into the target area. When resistance is expected or when it is to ensure the target area is sealed off, the search (or assault) element travels behind the security and support elements. 

5-105. The search (or assault) element normally divides into three types of teams: search teams, security teams, and support teams (see figure 5-4). Since these teams are most often in direct contact with the local populace and potential threats, these teams train and prepare accordingly. Teams within the search (or assault) element initiate actions once the outer and inner cordons are in place. Paragraphs 5-106 through 5-108 address each team’s actions. 

**Figure 5-4. Cordon and search (target area)** 

5-106. Search teams focus on the actual conduct of the search and the processes of site exploitation. They are not normally part of the security of the target area but can be when necessary. A search team relies on the support team for secondary tasks such as collected exploitable material and detainee handling. 

5-107. Security teams are responsible for gaining access to, clearing, and maintaining security of the immediate objective. They provide immediate security, protection, overwatch, and supervising movement into and out of the objective. Security teams are not tasked with any actions that would detract from security. In most cases, the existence of inner and outer cordons does not constitute local security for the search (or assault) element. 

5-108. Support teams are responsible for providing an organized force to conduct continuing actions in the objective area and to provide any necessary direct assistance to the search and security teams. Such actions may include detainee handling, collected exploitable material collection and handling, and casualty evacuation. 

5-109. During the establishment of the cordon, the search (or assault) element prepares to execute movement to the target and target area. Such movement may be immediate when arrival at the target and target area has been planned to coincide with the placement of the inner and outer cordons. Conversely, the search (or assault) element executes a short security halt at a designated position while it awaits deployment of the security element. Depending on the ingress point(s) (single or multidirectional), this may or may not occur in conjunction with the support element. 

5-110. During the search (actions on the objective) phase, the search (or assault) element moves into the target area and conducts the requisite actions to clear and search the target area. It clears the target area and sets up a permissive environment for a systematic search. The search may be targeted (specific to people, rooms, or buildings) or comprehensive (including everything in the target area). Tactical tasks associated with the search element include those following: 

- _Breach_ —a tactical mission task in which a unit breaks through or establishes a passage through an enemy obstacle (FM 3-90). 

- Clear—a tactical mission task in which a unit eliminates all enemy forces within an assigned area. 

- _Defeat_ —to render a force incapable of achieving its objectives (ADP 3-0). 

- _Destroy_ —a tactical mission task that physically renders an enemy force combat-ineffective until reconstituted (FM 3-90). 

- _Neutralize_ —a tactical mission task in which a unit renders the enemy incapable of interfering with an operation (FM 3-90). 

- _Seize_ —a tactical mission task in which a unit takes possession of a designated area by using overwhelming force (FM 3-90). 

- _Support by fire_ —a tactical mission task [in which a] unit engages the enemy by direct fire in support of another maneuvering force (FM 3-90). 

5-111. The search (or assault) element departs the target area under the overwatch of the security and support elements and generally serves as the lead element in the withdrawal order of movement. It normally retains that position throughout the rest of the withdrawal to enable command and control ease of withdrawal. 

###### **Support Element** 

5-112. By design, support elements act as a force multiplier during a cordon and search operation and are positioned where they can best accomplish assigned tasks. They may assist the cordon and search force by serving as a designated reserve, providing additional enabling teams to support all elements of the force, and conducting continuing actions such as establishing a temporary defensive position and conducting vehicle recovery, casualty evacuation, or resupply. 

5-113. The support element moves as either the second or third element of movement in the order of march. When resistance is not expected or when speed and surprise are paramount, it moves as the trail element— so as not to interfere with the security and search (or assault) elements’ movements—but remains positioned in support of actions on the objective. When resistance is expected or when it is to ensure the target area is sealed off, the support element travels as the second element to move into positions of support and security around the target area before the search element is committed. 

5-114. As actions on the objective occur, the support element executes its assigned tasks for the cordon and search force. It establishes secure positions in or near the target area appropriate for safely securing detainees, collected exploitable material, and casualties. Position placements are readily accessible to the cordon and search force and defendable against attack. The support element may provide extra detainee and collected exploitable material handling teams to the search (or assault) element, as well as internal resupply, vehicle recovery, and hasty repair capabilities. It may also conduct casualty evacuations. Often, it controls various enablers attached to the search (or assault) element until they are needed elsewhere. Tactical mission tasks associated with the support element include those following: 

- _Follow and assume_ —a tactical mission task in which a committed force follows and supports a lead force conducting an offensive operation and continues mission if lead force cannot continue (FM 3-90). 

- _Follow and support_ —a tactical mission task in which a committed force follows and supports a lead force conducting an offensive operation (FM 3-90). 

5-115. The support element, normally nested within the command element, follows in trace of the search (or assault) element and is the last of the cordon and search force to depart the target area, overwatched by the security element. During the withdrawal, depending on tasking, it may transport multiple detainees or large amounts of captured material, and it may tow damaged vehicles. 

#### **SEARCH AND ATTACK** 

5-116. _Search and attack_ is a variation of a movement to contact where a friendly force conducts coordinated attacks to defeat a distributed enemy force (FM 3-90). The conduct of this variation occurs when the enemy operates as small, dispersed elements whose locations cannot be determined to targetable accuracy by methods other than a physical search or when the task is to deny the enemy the ability to move inside a given area. A search and attack is normally conducted by dismounted or mounted Infantry forces, and it may be supported by Stryker and armored, equipped forces. It often occurs during the conduct of IW. However, it may also be necessary when conducting noncontiguous operations during combat operations and the consolidation of gains. These types of search and attack operations are normally characterized by robust reconnaissance and surveillance and by rapidly concentrated combat power to fix and finish (defeat or destroy) the enemy, once located. (See ATP 3-21.20 and ATP 3-21.10 for information on the search and attack variation.) 

##### **ORGANIZATION OF FORCES** 

5-117. The Infantry rifle company normally conducts search and attack operations as part of a battalion or larger element. However, depending on the METT-TC (I) variables, it may conduct the operation independently. For independent conduct, the company organizes (as would the Infantry battalion) with a reconnaissance, fixing, and finishing force—each with a specific purpose and task to accomplish—and the appropriate level of support from fire support, sustainment, and other combat enablers. As with a cordon and search operation, the commander employs existing base units (platoons and squads) to organize search and attack forces. 

###### **Reconnaissance Force** 

5-118. The company, as part of the battalion search and attack operation, uses information from reconnaissance forces and surveillance assets internal and external to the battalion (for example, scouts, snipers, crewed aircraft, UAS organic or tasked echelon specific platforms, EW assets) to find and potentially to fix a dispersed enemy. The size of the reconnaissance force is based on available intelligence about the size of enemy forces in the AO and the size of the AO in terms of both the geographical boundaries and civilian population inside those boundaries. The less known about the situation, the larger the reconnaissance force. Once the enemy is found, the reconnaissance force determines whether it has the combat power to fix the threat or whether the battalion or company must fix the enemy with its fixing force. 

###### **Fixing Force** 

5-119. The fixing force (usually a company-sized force when conducting as part of the battalion and a platoon when conducting search and attack at the company level) prevents the enemy from moving to or from a specific location until the enemy is engaged and destroyed. It must have enough combat power to isolate the enemy forces once the enemy is located. It positions prior to initiating the search and attack operation. Initial fixing position placements are based on the enemy situation and, more appropriately, pre-positioned where fixing forces would most likely support the finishing force. In preparation for contact made in other areas, fixing forces have procedures in place to facilitate their moving to where they can influence the fight. Once the threat is fixed, a fixing force determines its ability to conduct the attack the finishing force would normally execute. If it is unable, another unit designated as the finishing force would execute the assault. 

###### **Finishing Force** 

5-120. A finishing force engages and destroys the enemy force and is normally the main effort of the search and attack operation. Finishing forces require enough combat power to defeat those enemy forces located in the AO. They are responsive and require synchronization with all support forces to accomplish the desired end state. Procedures remain in place to facilitate the finishing force’s quick movement. Otherwise, the enemy can rapidly attrit the fixing force and immediately break contact before engagement by the finishing force. These procedures include graphic control measures, responsive means of transportation, and effective communication with the force in contact. 

##### **SEARCH AND ATTACK PLANNING AND PREPARATION** 

5-121. The search and attack variation is a decentralized movement to contact against an enemy operating in dispersed elements and requires multiple, coordinated patrols at company level and below. The battalion may conduct a search and attack operation as a coordinated, battalion-level operation or as decentralized, independent, company-level operations. Whether conducting a coordinated or decentralized operation, the battalion or company designates a main effort and supporting efforts that enable them to maintain the amount of flexibility the situation dictates. 

5-122. During planning and preparation, commanders consider the most influential METT-TC (I) variables to a search and attack mission. The military decision-making process (MDMP) at battalion level and troop leading procedures (TLP) at company level and below provide commanders and subordinate leaders with the framework for planning population-centric, distributed operations. Upon receiving or in anticipation of receiving the search and attack mission, commanders initiate the process by alerting all participants of pending planning requirements. This enables participants to determine the amount of time available for planning and preparation and how to abbreviate the MDMP or TLP appropriately. (See ATP 3-21.20 and FM 6-0 for information on planning in a time-constrained environment.) This process organizes the battalion and subordinate units in purpose and space and serves to focus the search and attack to one or more of the following purposes: 

- Destroy the enemy—render enemy units in the AO ineffective for combat. 

- Deny the area—prevent the enemy from operating unhindered in a given area (for example, in any area the enemy is using for a base camp or for logistic support). 

- Protect the force—prevent the enemy from massing to disrupt and destroy friendly military or civilian operations, equipment, and property such as key facilities, headquarters, or polling places. 

- Collect information—gain information about the enemy and the terrain to confirm the predicted enemy COA from the IPOE process. 

5-123. A commander’s situational understanding and knowledge of the higher echelon’s concept of operations enables the planning and development of a clear task and purpose for each subordinate force. As planning and preparation continue, the commander establishes control measures that allow for decentralized actions and small-unit initiative to the greatest extent possible. Minimum control measures for a search and attack operation are an AO, target reference points, objectives, checkpoints, and contact points. The use of target reference points facilitates responsive fire support once the reconnaissance (and surveillance) force makes contact with the enemy. Commanders use objectives and checkpoints to guide the movement of the subordinate elements. Contact points indicate a specific location and time for coordinating fires and movement between adjacent units. Commanders use other control measures such as phase lines and named areas of interest (AOIs) appropriately. 

5-124. Planning for the search and attack, based on the IPOE, combines the battalion intelligence staff officer’s (S-2’s) pattern and predictive analysis with available higher echelon collected information to determine likely enemy locations, capabilities, patterns, and actions. As developed, this information passes to subordinate units in the form of intelligence products. The scheme of maneuver for the search and attack operation is developed to capitalize on this information and integrates internal and external fire support assets available to the battalion (and as required) down to the company and platoon. Fire support plans provide flexible and rapidly delivered fires to achieve the commander’s desired effects throughout the AO. Commanders position fire support assets to support subordinate elements throughout their AOs and establish procedures for rapidly clearing fires. To clear fires rapidly, CPs and subordinate commanders track and report the locations of all the subordinate elements. Due to the uncertain enemy situation, commanders assign clear fire support relationships. 

5-125. Synchronization of movement and maneuver, fire support, protection, and sustainment are difficult to achieve in this type of decentralized movement to contact. Distances between units, the terrain, and a vague enemy situation contribute to the difficulty. For these reasons, commanders position themselves where they can best receive information and transmit orders, and they shift and commit forces during the search and attack operation. CPs lie where they can best influence the battle and afford commanders the best vantage point of the battlespace, which may not necessarily exist with the main effort. When attached in a direct support role, air defense assets increase protection for CPs. They may also provide security to maneuver and sustainment units and overwatch key air and ground routes or avenues of approach. 

5-126. Fire support officers prepare the fire support plan for each phase of the search and attack operation and contingencies. They recommend the positioning of attached joint fires observers to support the operation and assist in deconflicting company and higher echelon airspace. Tactical air control parties’ positions lie well forward (within range of reconnaissance, fixing, and finishing forces) to increase the timeliness and accuracy of close air support. Key to air-ground integration during search and attack operations are the means to develop _combat identification_ , which is the process of attaining an accurate characterization of detected objects in the operational environment sufficient to support an engagement decision (JP 3-09). Priority of fires for the battalion mortars during the search and attack operation is normally to the main effort of the battalion. Company mortars employ organic fires to support the attack of the finishing force or to block ingress and egress routes, thereby preventing the enemy’s repositioning, in support of the fixing force. Finding the enemy may have both echelons initially providing priority of fires to the reconnaissance force. 

5-127. The battalion engineer staff officer’s expertise helps in the identification of breach points in enemy defenses and in the ensuring of mobility for the battalion and its subordinate units. Engineer assets from the divisional engineer battalion can augment the company to increase combat power and facilitate freedom of action. Engineers can conduct route reconnaissance, determine bridge classifications, and find or make necessary bypass routes. Route clearance engineers detect and neutralizes explosive ordnances and reduces obstacles along routes, enabling force mobility in search and attack AOs. When necessary, a breach squad from the divisional engineer battalion can be task-organized to the route clearance force with mine-clearing line charges. The breach section of the IBCT and Infantry (Airborne) BCT provides mine-clearing line charges. 

5-128. While the brigade aviation officer, who leads the brigade aviation element, works directly for the IBCT commander as a permanent member of the IBCT special staff, aviation liaison teams can represent the supporting aviation task force at designated maneuver headquarters for the duration of a specific operation. When co-located with a brigade aviation element, the liaison team normally works directly with the brigade aviation officer as a functioning addition to the brigade aviation element cell. The coordination and synchronization of search and attack operations requires the effective employment of liaison officers. Often, aviation liaison teams coordinate with the brigade aviation element and proceed to a supported ground maneuver battalion conducting the search and attack operation. Aviation units (attack and reconnaissance, assault, and lift) can reconnoiter, guide ground forces to the enemy, provide lift and fire support assets for air movement, direct artillery fires, aid in command and control, and protect exposed flanks. Attack and reconnaissance units can reinforce when antiarmor firepower becomes necessary to block or fix the enemy. 

5-129. The essential nature of communication to a battalion search and attack operation (characterized by dispersed, decentralized, independent, company-level operations) hints at an additional planning problem— communications. Their limited range in the type of complex terrain most associated with search and attack missions requires detailed planning and rehearsal to resolve any terrain-masking effects and distances. Relays or retransmission stations may be necessary, and as for the combat multipliers, additional planning is essential. All these considerations undergo a detailed preparation for combat, fleshing out during TLP (and MDMP) and pushing to higher in the form of requests for information or enablers. 

5-130. Assault platoons from the Infantry weapons company can augment the rifle company. When assault platoons (heavy weapons) are attached, the rifle company commander and heavy weapons commander coordinate the best use of the heavy weapons assets. Coordination with the battalion S-3 to select medium close combat missile system positions and TOW (tube-launched, optically tracked, wire- or wireless-guided) missile positions—for providing long-range direct fire support—occurs when the Infantry weapons company is operating organically. Based on analysis, the commander can use the MK19 or caliber .50 machine gun in place of or in combination with the TOW missile system. The weapons company can also provide mobility and additional firepower for security missions and the reserve. During limited visibility, the weapons company with advanced optics can augment security forces at key locations, monitoring areas where the enemy is expected to travel at night. 

##### **SEARCH AND ATTACK EXECUTION** 

5-131. During execution, commanders focus their efforts on translating decisions made during planning and preparation into actions. To accomplish the search and attack mission successfully, a commander applies appropriate combat power at the correct time and location for gaining and maintaining a position of relative advantage. To seize, retain, and exploit the initiative, commanders ensure the synchronization of decentralized operations by specifying where each subordinate unit will operate, establishing measures to consolidate units before attacks, and establishing fire control measures for each subordinate unit. Commanders seek the most likely enemy locations, designate the forces most likely to make contact as the main effort, and prepare to shift the main effort appropriately. Search and attack forces, at battalion or company echelon, enter the AO by infiltrating as an entire unit or as smaller units via ground, air, or water. Finally, battalion and company operations do not end at the destruction of the enemy. Units immediately conduct consolidation and reorganization and prepare for follow-on offensive or defensive missions.

###### **Search and Attack—Separate Company Areas of Operations** 

5-132. For Infantry rifle companies operating in separate company AOs (see figure 5-5), one technique is to organize to find (perform reconnaissance), fix, and finish (destroy) the enemy within their capabilities. The battalion commander may retain a battalion reserve or direct each company to retain a reserve. The battalion’s indirect fire support is positioned to respond to all companies as needed. The commander employs the reserve, priority of fire, and other available assets to weight the main effort. Once the company reconnaissance force finds the enemy, the company commander concentrates combat power to fix and finish the enemy quickly. 

**Figure 5-5. Search and attack (company areas of operations)** 

5-133. Should the subordinate platoon be unable to destroy the detected enemy, the commander considers means to fix or contain the enemy. The commander may divert another platoon to the task, or the battalion commander might redirect another company or employ the battalion reserve or fires to contain and destroy the enemy. The commander redirects and repositions reconnaissance and surveillance assets to support any change to the plan and to identify enemy counterattack forces entering the AO. As plans change, the battalion commander provides control but allows for decentralized actions and small-unit initiative. 

###### **Search and Attack—Battalion Area of Operations** 

5-134. When the Infantry battalion operates in an AO, the commander may task-organize subordinate units to find (perform reconnaissance), fix, and finish (destroy) the enemy, each with a specific purpose and task to accomplish. Alternatively, the battalion commander may— - Task units with the reconnaissance efforts in assigned AOs and task individual subordinate elements with performing the fixing and finishing functions based on the situation.

- Direct subordinate companies to conduct reconnaissance and the fixing function in assigned AOs with the commander retaining direct control of the finishing force. 

- Rotate subordinate elements through the reconnaissance, fixing, and finishing functions, though rotating roles can require a change in task organization and additional time for rehearsal. 

5-135. During execution, the battalion commander ensures fire support and protection assets support the main effort while remaining responsive to the rest of the battalion. When the mortar platoon cannot support the entire battalion’s AO, the commander may consider splitting the platoon into sections. The commander considers the size of the area in which to conduct the search and attack operation, the number of available forces, and the time available. As the battalion staff conducts analysis to establish the duration of the mission, the staff assesses the battalion’s ability to conduct continuous operations, so they may develop and resource a plan to maintain the battalion’s combat effectiveness. Subordinate company and platoon unit tasks or actions, performed during the search and attack operation, may include the following actions: 

- Locating enemy positions or those routes normally traveled by the enemy. 

- Destroying enemy forces within the unit’s capability. 

- Fixing or blocking the enemy until reinforcements arrive. 

- Maintaining surveillance of a larger enemy force through stealth until reinforcements arrive. 

- Establishing ambushes. 

- Searching towns or villages. 

- Securing military or civilian property or installations. 

- Acting as a reserve. 

- Developing the situation in a given area. 

###### **_Find the Enemy_** 

5-136. Ample time is dedicated to determining the pattern of enemy operations. The commander is most effective once the pattern has been identified. However, accurately establishing an enemy pattern may take more time than is available. When conducting a search and attack operation, reconnaissance forces expect to spend significant time reconnoitering in an AO. The commander may consider using one of several techniques to find the enemy and may subdivide an AO into smaller ones. The scout platoon reconnoiters forward of the remainder of the battalion. Snipers and UAS organic or tasked echelon-specific platforms may reinforce the rifle company and scout platoon for this operation. The commander develops a contingency plan to prepare for any compromise of the reconnaissance force and to position the company to support. 

5-137. A search and attack operation with the scout platoon (or other security element) forward is one technique the Infantry battalion can use to find the enemy (see figure 5-6). In this illustration, the scout platoon conducting zone reconnaissance in AO Green initiates this method while the remainder of the battalion conducts search and attack operations in AO Blue. Serving as part of the reconnaissance force, the scout platoon attempts to obtain information about the enemy, initially in AO Green and then in AO Red. 

**Figure 5-6. Search and attack (scout platoon forward)** 

5-138. At a designated time, the battalion commander may direct the battalion to link up with the scout platoon at contact point 1 to exchange information. As necessary, the scout platoon guides the battalion to sites of suspected or confirmed enemy activity. When a scout platoon successfully locates the enemy, the battalion postures to attack. When the unit has not yet located the enemy, the battalion occupies AO Green and continues to search for the enemy. The scout platoon then moves to reconnoiter AO Red. 

5-139. The process continues until the unit locates and destroys the enemy force, the battalion’s AO is deemed free of enemy activity, or the commander terminates it. When the area is free of enemy activity, another AO is designated, and the process begins again. The commander may decide to emplace available sensors along the border from AO Red to AO Blue to identify enemy attempts to evade the battalion. An Infantry squad and a sniper team are tasked to emplace and monitor the sensors. 

5-140. The successive method of reconnaissance, in which the scout platoon reaches its AO before the remainder of the battalion, affords the scout platoon more opportunities to gain information on enemy activity in the area. It also helps the battalion commander focus the search and attack operation when the battalion moves to the new area. Caches or airdrops most often provide logistic support for the scout platoon. 

**_Note_ .** The Infantry battalion rarely designates the scout platoon as the finding force or a potential fixing force. The scout platoon is organized to find information and the enemy, not to become decisively engaged with the threat. Rifle companies typically serve as finding and fixing forces. 

5-141. Enemy operations over a very large area and in a decentralized manner force a battalion to disperse to locate and then mass to destroy the enemy. When possible, a battalion commander may enhance the units’ ability to mass combat power by keeping search areas relatively small and minimizing the requisite distance for moving the fixing and finishing force upon enemy contact. (See figure 5-7 for a battalion dispersing units to search and figure 5-8 for a company dispersed in a decentralized manner to conduct a search.) 

**Figure 5-7. Search and attack (unit dispersing to conduct a search)Figure 5-8. Search and attack (company dispersing to conduct a search)**

###### **_Fix the Enemy_** 

5-142. Once the reconnaissance force finds the enemy force, the fixing force develops the situation and executes one of two options, depending on the commander’s guidance and the METT-TC (I) variables. The first option is to block identified enemy escape and reinforcement routes. The second option is to conduct an attack to fix the enemy in its current position until the finishing force arrives. 

5-143. When blocking enemy escape and reinforcement routes, the fixing force maintains contact and positions its forces to isolate the enemy, to prevent the enemy from moving to a position of advantage, and to prevent the interdiction of reinforcements. These actions facilitate the conduct of attack by the finishing force. Control measures and communications remain established between closing units to prevent fratricide. UAS organic or tasked echelon-specific platforms can assist in preventing fratricide by observing forward of the moving units and identifying friendly and enemy units as they approach. 

5-144. When conducting an attack, the fixing force fixes the enemy in its current position until the finishing force arrives. Sniper fires are useful for disrupting the enemy and containing movement as the finishing force approaches. The fixing force can conduct the finishing attack when it is consistent with the commander’s intent with respect to tempo and when the available forces can generate the necessary combat power. Depending on the enemy’s mobility and the likelihood of the reconnaissance force’s compromise, the commander may need to position the fixing force before the reconnaissance force enters the AO. 

**_Note_ .** When conditions are not right for the finishing force to attack the detected enemy, the fixing force and reconnaissance force can continue to conduct reconnaissance and surveillance activities to develop the situation further. The fixing force continues to avoid detection and reports the enemy order of battle and activities. It uses stealth in this effort, carefully avoids an enemy ambush, and always retains the ability to fix the enemy. 

###### **_Finish the Enemy_** 

5-145. Ultimately, the purpose of the search and attack is to destroy the enemy. Reconnaissance forces find the enemy; fixing forces rapidly fix the enemy as finishing forces mass combat power to facilitate the enemy’s destruction. Massing combat power incorporates combined arms. To apply combat power decisively, ethically, effectively, and efficiently, the commander makes timely decisions, issues mission-type orders, and communicates with subordinate leaders to gather and disseminate information. During the execution of the search and attack, the commander locates the best position for obtaining information and reacting to subordinate unit contacts with appropriate force. 

5-146. A movement to contact anticipates a roughly linear arrangement between moving and stationary forces—that is, movement in one general direction. This may or may not be the case for the search and attack variation. During the conduct of a search and attack operation out of a centrally located CP or base, the commander’s control becomes more complex. The commander may remain centrally located with the reserve and mortars to ensure immediate, responsive fire support to any subordinate unit who makes contact with the enemy. Additionally, rather than moving positions with the main effort, the commander’s central position may enable a more rapid response to the decisive point where contact is made. Otherwise, the commander may not be in contact or communication with a supporting effort upon enemy contact. Once a supporting effort’s search activity finds the enemy, it can quickly become the main effort. 

5-147. As the situation develops, decentralized operations may require the establishment of additional fire support positions to provide responsive fires to subordinate units conducting search and attack. Fire support units provide fire support coverage inside a complete, 360-degree circle. This situation requires significantly different control measures and greater planning detail due to the wide variety encountered in observer target and gun-to-target angles. Decentralized operations may drive situations in which finishing forces conduct point or area ambushes and use fires to drive the enemy into those ambushes. Such fires require the establishment of restrictive fire areas, coordinated fire lines, or no-fire areas around or between positions of adjacent ambush units in the AO. 

5-148. The commander may move the finishing force behind the reconnaissance and fixing forces or may locate the finishing force at a pickup zone to conduct an air assault into a landing zone near the enemy once the enemy is located. The finishing force remains responsive enough to engage the enemy before the enemy can break contact with the reconnaissance force or the fixing force. The battalion intelligence officer provides the commander with an estimate of the time it will take the enemy to displace from its detected locations. The commander provides additional mobility assets, so the finishing force can respond within that timeframe. When established, the main effort is weighted by the commander by way of priority of fires and assigned priorities of support to available combat multipliers such as engineer elements and helicopter lift support. The commander establishes any necessary control measures to consolidate units and concentrate the combat power of the force before the attack. 

5-149. The commander employs the finishing force to destroy the enemy by conducting an attack as a hasty or deliberate operation, maneuvering to block enemy escape routes while another unit conducts the attack, or employing indirect fire or close air support to destroy the enemy (see figure 5-9). The commander may have part of the fixing force establish an area ambush and then have the reconnaissance and remaining fixing forces drive the enemy into the ambush, establish a reserve, and screen the objective area. 

**Figure 5-9. Search and attack (unit massing to attack)** 

##### **SECTION III – OFFENSIVE ENABLING TASKS AND ACTIVITIES** 

5-150. Offensive enabling tasks and activities empower and complement the other COIN LOEs (for example, civil security, civil control, support to HNSF, support to governance). Without the increased security resulting from offensive operations, units may not be able to accomplish any significant tasks in the other LOEs. Establishing civil security promotes a safe environment. Establishing civil control regulates select behavior and activities of individuals and groups. It also reduces risk to individuals and groups and provides security from both external and internal threats. Together, actions along these LOEs in COIN often take the form of unilateral and combined offensive operations against insurgent leaders, guerrillas, underground elements, and auxiliary forces. These offensive actions help establish public order and safety. In addition to effective targeting (see chapter 4, section IV), offensive operations are more successful when key enabling tasks and activities support them. Key enabling tasks and activities include search operations, site exploitation, sniper operations, patrolling, scheme of fires, and UAS employment. 

#### **SEARCH OPERATIONS** 

5-151. A search is the deliberate examination of a person, place, area, or object by Soldiers or animals or with technological sensors to discover something or someone. Searches may be of enemy or detained personnel, military objective areas, personnel or vehicles at checkpoints, and lines of communication. 

##### **SITUATIONS FOR AND PURPOSES OF SEARCHES** 

5-152. The conduct of a search can occur under a wide variety of situations and for a wide variety of purposes. Typically, the purpose of searching an individual, place, area, and object such as a desk is to find whatever they conceal. (See chapter 7 for information on vehicle searches.) Searches through communications from letters, books, computers, smartphones, and other media and signaling tools are for discovering information. 

5-153. During a COIN, the ROE and various agreements between the HN and U.S. COIN forces often describe search situations and limit search methods. Informing the local populace, as much as tactically possible, that the search contributes to their safety and security is important. This communication begins during the search, and often, follow-up patrols continue it after the search. Follow-up patrols not only aid in mitigating negative aspects of the search but also check for the return of missed individuals to the searched area. Those including CA teams or tactical PSYOP teams are capable of conducting consequence management, assisting in the achievement of information engagement (often through reinforcing themes), and collecting information for development into intelligence. 

##### **TECHNIQUES FOR SEARCH OPERATIONS** 

5-154. A search can orient on people, materiel, buildings, or terrain. Key considerations for conducting a search include the searching and detention of individuals, the searching of subterranean areas, aerial searches, tactical site exploitation, tactical questioning, and detainee processing. 

###### **Individuals** 

5-155. Any individual may be a member of the insurgency, an auxiliary force, or the mass base. However, searchers avoid mistaking all suspects for the enemy. Due to the potential lack of HN personnel identification procedures, correctly identifying a person as an insurgent can prove very difficult. The initial handling of individuals undergoing a search requires the greatest caution. During the search, one member of the search team always covers the other member, who performs the actual search. When females undergo a search, the search team takes every precaution to prevent violating local mores. When the unit can provide no female searchers, it employs the medic to search the female suspects. 

###### **Teams** 

5-156. Soldiers conduct individual searches in search teams. These teams employ the following members: the searcher actually conducts the search, thereby assuming the highest risk; security maintains eye contact with the person the searcher is searching; the observer supervises the search and warns the team of suspicious behavior or actions. 

###### **Methods** 

5-157. The most common search methods for searching an individual are frisk and wall searches. A third, less common method—useful in very select situations—is the strip search. A frisk search is quick and adequate for detecting weapons, collected exploitable material, or contraband. Yet, it is more dangerous since searchers have less control over the individuals they are searching. A wall search affords more safety for the searcher since the suspect is leaning against an upright surface such as a wall, vehicle, tree, or fence. For even greater safety, the kneeling and prone positions afford more control for searching an uncooperative individual. A strip search is an extreme measure conducted only when individuals are suspected of carrying documents or contraband on their persons, only in an enclosed area, and only by qualified personnel. A search with sensors such as metal detectors or thermals reveals hidden items. 

###### **Populace Control** 

5-158. Three basic methods are useful in populace control during a search of an urban area. These are assembling residents in a central location, restricting them to their residences, and controlling the heads of households. 

###### **_Assemble Residents in a Central Location_** 

5-159. This method moves residents from their residences to a central area. It provides the most control, simplifies a thorough search, denies insurgents an opportunity to conceal collected exploitable material, and allows for tactical questioning. However, this method has the disadvantage of taking residents away from their dwellings and possibly encouraging looting, which, in turn, engenders ill feelings. A specific element is identified to control the centralized populace. A tactical PSYOP team using a loudspeaker can facilitate assembly by giving specific instructions to the residents in the search area. 

###### **_Restrict Residents to Their Dwellings_** 

5-160. This technique prohibits the movement of civilians, allows them to stay in their dwellings, and discourages looting. The use of a tactical PSYOP team to broadcast the messages for staying indoors aids in clearing the streets of civilians and restricting their movement. The security element enforces this restriction to ensure compliance. The disadvantages of this method are the difficulty it adds to control and to tactical questioning and the time it affords inhabitants to conceal contraband in their residences. 

###### **_Control Heads of Households_** 

5-161. The head of each household is told to remain in front of the house while everyone else in the house is brought to one room. The security element controls the group at the central location, controls the head of each household, and provides external security for the search team. Of great importance when interacting with the head of a household is explaining the purpose of the search; thus, of equal importance is engaging an interpreter in this effort. During the search, the head of the household accompanies the search team through the house. This person may open doors and containers to facilitate the search. The head of the household is to see the search team steals nothing. 

###### **Houses or Buildings** 

5-162. The object of a house search is to look for contraband and to screen residents as potential members of guerrilla or auxiliary forces, an underground element, or the mass base. A search party who is assigned to search an occupied building comprises at least one local police officer, a protective escort for local security, and a female searcher. When inhabitants are to remain in the dwellings, the protective escort isolates and secures the inhabitants during the search. Forced entry may be necessary when a house is vacant or an occupant refuses to allow the searchers to enter. When the force is to search a house containing property while its occupants are away, it secures the house to prevent looting. Before U.S. Forces depart, the commander arranges for the community to protect such houses until the occupants return. 

5-163. One objective is to leave the house in the same condition as when the search began. In addition to information collection, the search team may use digital cameras or video recorders to establish the condition of the house before and after the search. All sensitive material or equipment found in the house is documented before it is removed to include the date, time, location, name of person from whom it was confiscated, and reason for the confiscation. The use of a digital camera can assist in the documentation process as well. For a detailed search, the walls and floors undergo searching to discover hidden caches. 

#### **SITE EXPLOITATION** 

5-164. _Site exploitation_ is the synchronized and integrated application of scientific and technological capabilities and enablers to answer information requirements, facilitate subsequent operations, and support host-nation rule of law (ATP 3-90.15). Tactical leaders plan, resource, direct, and supervise tactical site exploitation efforts during all COIN offensive operations. (See ATP 3-90.15 for information on site exploitation.) 

##### **CORE ACTIVITIES FOR SITE EXPLOITATION** 

5-165. Commanders and staffs use the core activities to understand, visualize, and describe site exploitation. In general, units implement the majority of site exploitation core activities on site. The ability of the unit to use presumptive analysis tools on site allows the commander to comprehend, decide, and react within the threat’s decision cycle. Commanders balance the performance of the site exploitation activities against the METT-TC (I) variables to determine the extent and viability of actions on the objective and beyond. Tactical site exploitation activities include those efforts necessary to complete the five core activities to the greatest extent possible within the constraints of time, available personnel, risk management (RM), and Soldier safety. (See ATP 3-90.15 for information on each core activity.) Site exploitation core activities are to detect, collect, process, analyze, and disseminate. 

###### **Detect** 

5-166. Detection entails a Soldier’s discovery or notice of pertinent information, materiel, or persons. Commanders and staffs develop and maintain information requirements to establish what information, materiel, or people to detect. 

###### **Collect** 

5-167. Collection activities occur mainly at the site or on the objective. Collection entails gathering, protecting, organizing, documenting, and controlling information and materiel and holding any persons detected at the site. 

###### **Process** 

5-168. Processing involves the protecting of detained personnel, material, and data from the point of collection and for as long as individuals are held and material and data hold intelligence or evidentiary value. Processing may occur for personnel and in the preparation and conversion of materiel and data into a suitable form for analysis. 

###### **Analyze** 

5-169. Analysis studies an object in detail for the purpose of explanation. The analysis of the collected information, materiel, and persons found at the site or on the objective evaluates their relationship to the site and supports deductions as to their probable meaning. 

###### **Disseminate** 

5-170. Dissemination entails the horizontal and vertical sharing of information and intelligence across supported and supporting organizations. This activity includes supporting knowledge management tasks. 

##### **SITE EXPLOITATION EXECUTION** 

5-171. Site exploitation is a systematic action executed with the appropriate equipment to ensure personnel, documents, electronic data, and other material at a site are identified, evaluated, collected, and protected and thereby to gather intelligence and facilitate follow-on actions. It is a means by which tactical units exploit and analyze the insurgent after collecting biometric, physical, digital, and spoken data. In COIN, insurgents who are captured many times are prosecuted IAW the host-nation rule of law, and site exploitation is an excellent means of providing courts with evidence, especially when properly recorded. Site exploitations contribute to the decide, detect, and assess functions of the decide, detect, deliver, and assess (D3A) targeting cycle (see chapter 4, section IV). Once collected, analyzed, and assessed, the evidentiary intelligence may lead to future operations. (See figure 5-10 for an example site exploitation sketch.) 

**Figure 5-10. Site exploitation sketch, example** 

##### **IDENTIFY, PRESERVE, AND COLLECT EXPLOITABLE MATERIAL** 

5-172. Leaders ensure Soldiers methodically and effectively identify, preserve, and collected exploitable material while maintaining its integrity. They strive to prevent damage or corruption from foreign materials, undocumented chains of custody, or loss. They mitigate risk by allowing a minimum of personnel to operate in the area, minimizing time on target, concealing the movement of collected exploitable material, avoiding patterns, and maintaining an obvious respect for civilians and their belongings. 

5-173. An important site exploitation resource, biometric assets can measure physical details of a human face, fingerprint, hand geometry, handwriting, iris, retina, vein, voice, and deoxyribonucleic acid (also called DNA). Other site exploitation resources include search, detention, and marking tools; collected exploitable material kits; marking materials; photographic, video recording, and voice recording devices; linguists; and artificial sources of light. In addition, leaders— 

- Initially evaluate the situation. 

- Decide whether the unit must perform an expedient or formal site exploitation. 

- Properly bag and tag evidence. 

- Record sworn statements from Soldiers and locals for entry into the legal system. 

**_Note_ .** Collected exploitable material kits provide the best and easiest way for leaders to complete the preceding two tasks. 

- Photograph captured contraband evidence alongside the suspect for judicial proceedings. 

- Ensure the photo documentation of people, materiel, and other items of intelligence interest and collected exploitable material collection occurs on or adjacent to the site. 

- Use document and media exploitation (DOMEX) (which includes the hasty analysis of pocket contents), electronic content from mirror imaging, and data evacuation for further, more detailed analysis. 

- Process detainees into a detainee holding area (DHA), including the collection of biometric and computer database information by special BCT-level teams. 

- Ensure the entry of pre- and post-bomb-blast forensics and signatures from improvised explosive device (IED) factories, which are routinely collected by weapons intelligence teams, into the IED system of record for comparison and analysis with detainee records. 

##### **TECHNIQUES FOR SITE EXPLOITATION** 

5-174. Using proper techniques is crucial during detect, collect, process, analyze, and disseminate activities. Basic site exploitation techniques include search methods, searches of individuals, detention of individuals, tactical questioning, and debriefing. 

###### **Methods of Searching Individuals** 

5-175. Search methods include security provisions for search teams, integrity preservation of the site, the conduct of a methodical search, and coherent documentation for later review. The type of employed search team depends on many factors such as available forces, HN capabilities, and the purpose of the search. The METT-TC (I) variables cover most of these. The following site exploitation on target checklist is not all inclusive: 

- Search all rooms, caves, roofs, yards, subterranean areas, and associated vehicles for the following items: 

 - Identification cards. 

 - Weapons. 

 - Computers. 

 - Documents. 

 - Digital media. 

 - Propaganda. 

 - Cellular and satellite phones. 

 - Large amounts of money. 

- Search other likely hiding places such as those following: 

 - Appliances (refrigerator, including the ice cube trays and under and inside the back housing). 

 - Furniture-related hide spots (inside cushions or hollow legs; taped to the back, sides, or bottom of furniture pieces). 

 - Floors (especially those with removable boards or tiles, with rugs, or that are hollow). 

 - Gardens, false walls, and chimneys. 

- Search all vehicles for weapons and photograph the weapons. 

- Positively identify the target. 

- Photograph all individuals. 

- Complete packets on all individuals. 

- Verify individuals by checking identification cards. 

- Perform a gunpowder test or other explosive field test on all individuals. 

- Photograph each detainee with affiliated collected exploitable material. 

- Collect and document all collected exploitable material and take it to the transport vehicle. 

- Load all detainees for transit to forward operating base (FOB), combat outpost, patrol base, or detention control point. 

###### **Detention of Individuals** 

5-176. A _detainee_ is any person captured, detained, or otherwise under the control of Department of Defense personnel (JP 3-31). The reasons for the capture or detention and the ultimate disposition and categorization of a detainee depend on the situation. Before detaining someone, a leader first decides what to do with the person afterward. Does the leader want to search, question, process, or release the person? 

5-177. AR 190-8, FM 3-63, and international law (including the law of war and Geneva Conventions) cover policies, procedures, and responsibilities for the administration, treatment, protection, security, and custody transference of detainees. They also cover other planning factors, as well as regulatory and legal requirements, concerning detainees. 

###### **_Detainee Processing Rules_** 

5-178. The six rules for processing detainees follow: 

- Search detainees thoroughly and disarm them. 

- Silence detainees. 

- Segregate detainees by sex and rank. 

- Safeguard detainees from harm while preventing their escape. 

- Speed detainees to designated detainee collection points. 

- Tag detainees by the approved format and with key information such as the date of capture, location of capture (grid coordinates), capturing unit, and special circumstances of capture (how each person was captured). 

###### **_Protected Status_** 

5-179. Once suspected insurgents are under friendly control, they assume the protected status of detainees. The term _detainee_ includes any person captured or otherwise detained by armed forces. Under the law of war, leaders and Soldiers are personally responsible for detainees in their control. Mistreatment of detainees is a criminal offense under the Geneva Convention Relative to the Treatment of Prisoners of War (GPW), or the Third Geneva Convention, and Title 18, United States Code, War Crimes, also known as the War Crimes Act of 1996. One of the most conspicuous violations of the GPW is unauthorized photography of detainees. 

**_Note_ .** U.S. Forces avoid photographing detainees for nonmilitary or unofficial purposes. Doing so is unauthorized. 

###### **Tactical Questioning** 

5-180. Units recognize the value of timely information and intelligence during COIN operations and, thus, may tactically question an insurgent on the objective. Units designate or construct a DHA, ensuring detainees are unable to communicate between each other in any manner. Leaders then conduct tactical questioning of priority detainees away from the group. They carefully gather the necessary facts and details to establish consistencies or inconsistencies. Leaders sort detainees into those to be taken off target, those without further value, those no longer of interest, and those who require immediate battlespace interrogation by qualified personnel. Leaders wanting the ability to interrogate personnel during a potential operation request and incorporate qualified interrogators into their mission task organization to facilitate timelier information. 

###### **_Necessity for Soldier Presence_** 

5-181. The terminology may change, but the need remains for Soldiers at the point of capture or of detainment to ask questions. Trained interrogators are seldom on hand, but Soldiers are always present. Experiences from recent operations show that U.S. Forces using immediate tactical questioning techniques with Soldiers on target find important information that leads to intelligence of immediate tactical value. Tactical questioning never violates the law of war or any legal agreements (status-of-forces agreements and coalition agreements). Typical questions focus on discovering other nearby insurgents, their intentions, their equipment, how they are financed, or their means of support. 

###### **_Backtracking of Route_** 

5-182. A successful technique for determining where individuals were before they came to the point of capture is to have them verbally backtrack their routes. Detainees are to answer questions about the timing of their arrival, how they traveled (for example, by foot or vehicle) to the point of capture, and from what direction. A general direction and a means of travel are enough to develop a route. Using a map, the Soldier asks leading questions to determine the route. A detainee identifies significant terrain features seen at specific locations, such as rivers, bridges, key buildings, or hills. Talking jogs a detainee’s memory. Gradually, detainees reveal their routes and origin points. Considerations for successful tactical questioning follow:

- Know the linguist and employ more than one to doublecheck the accuracy of the information and the integrity and reliability of the linguist. 

- Possess basic proficiency in the detainees’ languages. 

- Learn to identify physical behaviors and postures, including resistant and defensive, with the employment of multiple observers. 

- Study targets before they become detainees on the objective. 

- Study the behaviors, values, and interests of others in the OE before conducting tactical questioning. 

- • Consider placing a uniformed linguist among the detainees and allowing detainees to communicate so the uniformed linguist can collect information (deception collection). 

- Conduct the questioning of individuals separately from other detainees in case the detainee maintains plausible deniability with community members. 

- Commanders can prepare four to five questions related to information requirements that can then be briefed as part of the patrol order and used by leaders during operations. 

- Prepare a tactical questioning plan for information detainees may have. 

###### **Aerial Searches** 

5-183. UAS organic or tasked echelon-specific platforms, close air support, and rotary-wing aircraft (attack and reconnaissance units) serve well as observation platforms. Close air support aircraft and attack reconnaissance aviation can also provide commanders an aerial search capability with different search perspectives and constraints. Rotary-wing aircraft are an effective means of conducting mounted search patrols, specific populace control measures, and security operations. 

5-184. Helicopter-mounted patrols may reconnoiter an assigned area or route in search of insurgent elements. They may conduct snap checkpoints on roads to interdict mounted and dismounted insurgent movement. When the element locates a known or suspected element, it may instruct attack aviation teams to engage the insurgent element, or it may land and attack the enemy with a dismounted assault. This technique can be useful in open rural areas unless an air defense threat is present. Operations employ aerial patrols when sufficient intelligence is available to justify their employment or when friendly ground-based operations have become predictable to the insurgents. Such patrols are most effective in conjunction with ground operations. 

5-185. In aerial or air-ground search operations, helicopters insert troops in an area suspected of containing insurgents. With helicopters overwatching from the air, Soldiers search the area. Soldiers remount, and the process repeats in other areas. Aerial patrol members maintain training in tracking procedures to follow insurgents to their bases or safe houses, using the terrain, deception, the standoff capability of aviation optics, and ground and other technological assets. Leaders plan for the evacuation of prisoners, casualties, and materials, both by air and ground. 

###### **Subterranean Area Searches** 

5-186. In both urban and rural areas, insurgents remain undetected to survive. Therefore, insurgents use all means of concealment available. Subterranean areas, in both rural and urban areas, reduce the chance of detection and facilitate insurgent movement. Subterranean areas include natural caves, basements, underground bunkers, tunnels, holes, and sewer systems. Underground sewers and tunnels are also useful in the attack of targets and for egress after an attack. (See ATP 3-34.81 for information on tunnel [and subterranean] detection, reconnaissance, maneuver, and destruction.) 

###### **_Signs of Use of Subterranean Area_** 

5-187. Certain signs reveal the use of subterranean structures by insurgency forces in a specific area. Such indications include the following: 

- Movement of insurgents in a specific direction. 

- Sniper fire occurring from areas without obvious avenues of withdrawal. 

- HUMINT reports of subterranean areas. 

- Failure of cordons to prevent withdrawal or infiltration of insurgency forces. 

- Turned or managed soil far away from places of habitation or daily labor. 

- Operations during which insurgents inflict casualties and withdraw without detection or engaging COIN forces. 

- The smell of burning wood or food cooking in an uninhabited area. 

- Mounds of dirt and dirt of different colors, both of which might indicate digging. 

- Trails to water sources in uninhabited areas, which might indicate personnel requiring water. 

###### **_Methodical and Coordinated Approach_** 

5-188. Searching an area with suspected subterranean facilities requires a methodical and coordinated approach. The size of the surface area and the suspected size of the subterranean area determine the size and strength of the assigned unit. The unit is task-organized for subterranean search operations and divided into five elements: command and control, security, search, guard, reserve. The command and control element often remains with the reserve element. 

###### **_Narrowing of the Search_** 

5-189. To detect or locate subterranean facilities, leaders first reduce the geographical AOI to smaller areas of probable locations. Part of the process may entail the following activities: acquiring existing blueprints, maps, imagery, video recordings, aerial photographs, and hydrological analysis tools; actively observing for indicators of probable subterranean access locations; and questioning the local populace as to the existence or their specific knowledge of any subterranean area. Overhead imagery may produce results when the appearance of the surface and vegetation have changed or when deductions about substructures are possible from analysis of existing versus historical terrain. 

###### **_Security During Area Searches_** 

5-190. Perimeter and flank security are imperative. A slow, methodical search is conducted in the AO, with each search team systematically searching every square meter. The security element moves toward the limits of advance of the search area. Deliberate search techniques emphasize where to look for insurgent locations that would provide insurgents with observation, cover, concealment, and egress. 

###### **_Signs of Tunnels_** 

5-191. Several visible signs help in detecting the actual tunnels. Visual inspections often disclose the general area of a tunnel, though not its precise location. The keys to finding a tunnel system are thorough terrain analysis and an equally thorough physical ground search. 

###### **_Rural Visible Indications_** 

- 5-192. Visible indications in a rural OE include those following: 

 - Air holes. 

 - Worn places on trees an insurgent uses as handholds. 

 - A small trail, much like a game trail, through the brush into a clump of small trees. 

 - Cut trees and limbs tied near a treetop to conceal the use of a tunnel from aircraft. 

 - Slight depression in or around a group of small trees. 

 - A lone individual, especially a female, in the area. 

 - Freshly cooked food with no one attending the site. 

 - Fresh human feces in an area. 

###### **_Urban Visible Indications_** 

- 5-193. Visible indications in an urban OE include those following: 

 - Sewer, storm drain, or utility grates or manhole covers. 

 - Disturbed soil in mature gardens. 

 - Presence of flooring materials in residences, businesses, and other structures not under construction. 

#### **SNIPER OPERATIONS** 

5-194. Sniper operations are effective for both insurgents and counterinsurgents in the COIN environment. Snipers, when employed correctly, are a COIN force multiplier and provide the commander an immediate means to enter the insurgency’s decision-making cycle. (See ATP 3-21.20 and TC 3-22.10 for information on sniper operations.) 

**_Notes_ .** U.S. Army sniper squads and teams provide the commander with precise, long-range, and discriminatory fires. The sniper is especially valuable when fighting an enemy who is attempting to blend into the local population. Sniper targets designated by the commander may include the following: enemy leaders, specialists, and snipers; enemy personnel and other individuals as specified; and key enemy equipment and vehicles. The sniper element’s second mission is to collect and report accurate and detailed battlespace information. 

ATP 3-21.20 provides the doctrinal framework for the Infantry sniper squad and sniper employment officer (SEO) assigned to Infantry battalions in the IBCT. Appendix E works in conjunction with and complements TC 3-22.10. 

##### **SNIPER OPERATIONS OVERVIEW** 

5-195. During the conduct of offensive operations, through the depth of a COIN force’s AO, the primary mission of an assigned sniper element is to deliver precise long-range fire on selected targets. Sniper fires create a marked effect on insurgency forces—create casualties, slow activities, instill fear, influence their decisions and actions, lower morale, and add confusion to their operations. 

5-196. The sniper element’s observational and navigational skills and specialized equipment help it see the terrain in detail and observe changes. Snipers provide the commander with details about the terrain, obstacles, likely avenues of approach, and other pertinent battlespace information. 

5-197. Snipers infiltrate the insurgency’s areas to engage the enemy from unexpected directions. Employing snipers in advance of unit movement allows them to move at their own paces and thereby to remain undetected. During movement or from static positions, snipers attempt to identify insurgent positions or movements, provide overwatch, and engage insurgent targets who threaten the overall operation or protected element movement or position. (See paragraphs 6-150 through 6-182 for information on counter-sniper operations.) 

##### **SNIPER EMPLOYMENT OFFICER** 

5-198. The SEO is responsible for advising the commander, subordinate commanders, and staff on the employment and control of assigned snipers in the unit. For example, in the Infantry battalion, the SEO can be the headquarters and headquarters company commander, the XO, the scout platoon leader, or any other officer. In the SEO’s absence, either the sniper squad leader or the individual sniper team leader can perform this duty. Paragraphs 5-199 through 5-205 describe the specific duties of the SEO for the Infantry battalion to know, advise, coordinate, train, issue orders, supervise, and debrief (also called KACTIS-D) and provide examples for discussion purposes. 

5-199. The SEO maintains knowledge of sniper capabilities. The SEO understands employment considerations and the capabilities and limitations of sniper teams, including movement and camouflage techniques, observation techniques, hide site operations, and marksmanship. 

5-200. The SEO advises the supported commander, battalion S-3, and battalion S-2 on how to employ the sniper units (by squad, section, or team). In addition to sniper capabilities and limitations, the SEO ensures the commander sees the sniper as the eyes, ears, and trigger finger in the battlespace for the battalion. 

5-201. The SEO coordinates all aspects of the sniper mission. Coordination begins during mission analysis and is continuous throughout the operations process. The SEO coordinates the assignment of sniper teams to missions to support units or as an integrated part of a sniper mission. To prevent fratricide and possible compromise of position and mission, the SEO coordinates AO terrain management with units. 

5-202. The SEO maintains realistic, varied, challenging, and mission-oriented training. The SEO assembles the battalion sniper squad, including any snipers assigned to company sniper teams, to standardize training and SOPs. Every requisite skill for a sniper (including information collection) is perishable and takes continual practice. The SEO ensures snipers receive the proper time and resources for maintaining effectiveness in their skills. An experienced sniper squad leader serves as the SEO’s primary trainer. Concurrent sniper training at the IBCT level ensures standardized SEO and sniper training and SOPs across the IBCT. 

5-203. The SEO issues orders to any sniper squad and team leaders. The SEO issues the order to all applicable sniper squad and team leaders through an OPORD or fragmentary order (FRAGORD). 

5-204. The SEO supervises planning and preparation (specific to rehearsals and backbriefs). The SEO provides supervision for the planning of the mission, the preparation of the mission, and mission rehearsals. A good backbrief indicates the sniper squad’s or team’s readiness for the mission. 

5-205. The SEO debriefs all members of the team upon mission completion. The SEO, ICW the battalion S-2, conducts detailed debriefings after mission completion. Any sniper squads or teams bring all pertinent information (for example, their data books, sniper logs, field sketches, digital photos, DA Form 5517 [ _Standard Range Card_ ]) to the debriefing. 

##### **COUNTERINSURGENCY TASK, PERSONNEL, AND EQUIPMENT** 

5-206. Small kill teams (SKTs), small capture teams (SCTs), and small observation teams (SOTs) differ by task, personnel, and equipment. SKTs focus on destroying insurgent elements. SCTs focus on capturing insurgent elements. SOTs conduct reconnaissance. In COIN, more advantage may be gained by capturing than killing insurgents. However, SKTs can provide commanders with a deterrent to insurgent activity. 

5-207. Sniper teams, sometimes as part of SKTs, SCTs, or SOTs, are employed in populated urban areas or large rural areas with adequate fields of fire. For mission success, all three teams employ specific point and area weapon systems.
