6-157. Observation posts have access to powerful spotting telescopes, medium-power binoculars, night observation devices (thermal if possible), and remote-controlled, closed-circuit cameras. Additionally, laser countermeasures are employed, such as laser protective glasses, binoculars with laser filters, and indirect view optics to protect observers. Many electronic detection devices such as acoustic devices are available for detecting snipers. Once detected, snipers can then be neutralized or forced to withdraw. Observers maintain constant surveillance over potential sniper positions and detect snipers as they attempt to move into firing positions. Constantly scanning an area for the minute movements of a well-trained sniper is exhausting. Therefore, personnel on static observation post duty rotate frequently. An observation post plan integrates crewed aircraft and UAS organic or tasked echelon-specific platforms to add depth. 

###### **_Countermeasure Patrols_** 

6-158. Continuous reconnaissance and security patrols around a unit’s position hinder insurgent snipers from getting into firing positions undetected. Small-unit patrols are usually more effective than large ones. A moving insurgent sniper whom a patrol has discovered is at a great disadvantage since such a sniper lacks the firepower to fight a long engagement. Small night reconnaissance patrols with night-vision devices can be very effective in disrupting and interdicting a sniper. Reconnaissance patrols move by covered and concealed routes to good observation points, stop and observe, and then move to another position. Patrols vary their routes and times, and a reaction force or supporting weapons maintain readiness in case the patrol makes contact. A variation of the ambush patrol is the stay-behind ambush. A small ambush element moves as part of a larger patrol and occupies its position without being observed. It then observes its kill zone— which can be very large when the element has a sniper team with it—and engages enemy snipers as they attempt to move into position. Small kill teams (SKTs), small capture teams (SCTs), or small observation teams (SOTs) conduct ambushes of likely sniper positions and sniper infiltration and exfiltration routes. 

###### **_United States Army Sniper Squads and Teams_** 

6-159. U.S. Army sniper teams can be a very effective counter to enemy snipers. Not only do they have expert knowledge of sniping and likely enemy hiding places, but they also normally engage enemy snipers, marksmen, and markswomen at a greater range than the one at which the enemy sniper engages U.S. Forces. 

Their precision fires are also much less likely to cause civilian casualties than those from nonprecision weapons. 

###### **_Suppressive Fire While Maneuvering_** 

6-160. Before a unit encounters an enemy sniper, the unit has not only developed an understanding of the ROE but has also wargamed the ROE to ensure the authorized level of response is sufficient. Although the ROE and the tactical situation determine the response, authorization ideally includes the ability to respond with fires from all the unit’s light weapons. When a unit can determine the general location of a sniper, it returns suppressive fire while maneuvering to engage the sniper from close range. This maneuver is not always successful because a well-trained sniper often has chosen a route of withdrawal already. Fires without maneuver are not successful in defeating snipers. 

###### **_Obscurants_** 

6-161. Projected obscurants (handheld or from an M320 grenade launcher) that build quickly are a good response to enemy sniper engagement for protecting a unit from further casualties. Effective placement of obscurants by the unit leader greatly limits the insurgent sniper’s ability to acquire targets. The closer the obscurant is placed to the sniper’s location, the more effective it is. When the sniper’s location is unknown or cannot be reached by projected obscurants, an obscurant cloud established near the unit can be effective in reducing the sniper’s chances of hitting a target and allowing a unit to conduct casualty care under fire. (See ATP 3-21.8 for information on tactical combat casualty care.) 

###### **Passive Countermeasures** 

6-162. Passive countermeasures prevent an insurgent sniper from acquiring a clear target and sniper fires from causing casualties. Passive counter-sniper measures are rarely successful by themselves. If passive countermeasures are the only ones enacted, they might create a siege mentality and pass the initiative to the insurgent sniper. Paragraphs 6-161 through 6-165 review some passive countermeasures. 

###### **_Limiting Sniper Exposure_** 

6-163. Soldiers who limit their sniper exposure can marginalize insurgent sniper operations. Some examples include using covered and concealed routes, avoiding lighted areas at night, moving tactically while using traveling overwatch or bounding overwatch, and staying away from doors and windows. 

###### **_Wearing Personal Protective Equipment_** 

6-164. Personal protective equipment measures include the wearing of the body armor systems (including the helmet) and protective eyewear. Soldiers wear these whenever they are at risk of exposure to sniper fire. Doing so decreases an insurgent sniper’s casualty-producing target area and consequently the sniper’s effectiveness. (See ATP 3-21.8 for information on personal protective equipment postures.) 

###### **_Moving in Armored Vehicles_** 

6-165. Depending on the METT-TC (I) variables, Soldiers move around in the urban area in an armor-protected vehicle with as little exposure as possible. They avoid open-sided cargo vehicles. They requisition or improvise vehicular armor against small arms fire for all unarmored vehicles. This technique limits a unit’s ability for public interaction, so Soldiers employ it only when necessary. 

###### **_Erecting Screens and Shields_** 

6-166. Simple canvas or plastic screens make crossing a dangerous alleyway or street safer for foot traffic. Adapting screens on windows allows for outward visibility while hiding inside personnel. Moveable concrete barriers protect personnel at static positions. Common items such as sandbags or rubble-filled 55-gallon drums provide cover. 

###### **_Denying Enemy Use of Overwatching Terrain_** 

6-167. Units occupy overwatching terrain with friendly forces, or they modify it to render it less useful to an enemy sniper. Example modifications include removing likely hiding places, clearing bushes and rubble, boarding or bricking up windows, and piling earth and rubble in front of buildings to block lines of sight for snipers. However, units ensure all actions are IAW the laws of war. 

##### **COUNTER-SNIPER OPERATIONS AND TECHNIQUES** 

6-168. Counter-sniper operations work in conjunction with and complement techniques to eliminate insurgent snipers. During COIN operations, sniper elements are effective primarily because they can deliver selective, precision fires against specific targets IAW the ROE. Due to their skills in observation and their familiarity with their AOs, snipers play a vital role in providing information. Support to COIN-focused operations places an additional strain on the sniper to kill, without the motivational stimulus normally associated with the battlespace. During support to COIN-focused operations tasks, the sniper’s ROE may differ from those of the supported counterinsurgent unit. 

6-169. Sniper elements supporting COIN operations thoroughly plan any counter-sniper operation. During counter-sniper operations, snipers perform the following steps: 

- Determine the threat. 

- Gather information. 

- Determine patterns. 

- Determine the best location and time to engage the enemy. 

- Engage the enemy. 

6-170. The sniper employment officer (SEO) (see paragraph 5-198) is generally a position within the battalion operations section, and sniper element leader can perform the duties of the SEO. Both these positions receive notification of any report regarding the following: 

- Sightings of insurgent members wearing special camouflage uniforms. 

- Sightings of insurgent members carrying weapons with long barrels, mounted scopes, or bolt-action receivers or carrying weapon cases or drag bags. 

- Key personnel casualties such as commanders, senior noncommissioned officers (NCOs), or weapons crewmembers and a simultaneous reduction in enemy patrol activities. 

- Reports of reflections off optical lenses. 

- Intelligence or reconnaissance units detect small groups of insurgents (one to three personnel). 

- Findings of single, spent cartridges in calibers known for use by insurgent snipers. 

6-171. When an insurgent sniper is operating in the unit area, the sniper force or any other force uses countermeasures to protect the unit against sniper fire. These countermeasures fall under two categories: 

- Unit-level, counter-sniper, active measures:  Gather information. 

 - Make a plan. 

 - Observe likely locations. 

 - Locate insurgency forces through observation since stalking and tracking expose the team to higher risk. 

 - Kill the insurgent sniper. 

- Unit-level, counter-sniper, passive measures: 

 - Avoid routines such as consistent mealtimes, ammunition resupply times, assembly area procedures, patrol routes, routes to the objective rally point, or any other day-to-day activities. 

 - Gather, meet, and brief under cover or in limited visibility. 

 - Cover or conceal equipment such as maps, radios, and antennas. 

 - Remove rank and do not salute. 

 - (Leaders) Avoid behaving authoritatively. 

 - Increase the unit’s observation capabilities through such means as observation posts. 

 - Inform patrols to look for signs of the presence of a sniper, such as single, spent cartridges and camouflage materials other than those the unit uses. 

 - Do not dismiss the potential for a woman to be the sniper. 

6-172. Counter-sniper Soldiers apply field craft, camouflage, and movement techniques to infiltrate (or exfiltrate) concealed positions that increase the probability of delivering accurate fires onto a target. Their ability to engage point targets with accuracy, at long range, and with minimal risk of collateral damage makes them useful in the range of military operations. Counter-sniper Soldiers’ reconnaissance and surveillance training, long-range optics, and communication skills make them a valuable resource for information collection activities. Counter-sniper actions have two main parts: find the sniper and eliminate the sniper. 

###### **Find the Insurgent Sniper** 

6-173. Once a COIN unit determines it has an insurgent sniper or sniper team in its AO, the unit implements counter-sniper, immediate action drills. Allowing the enemy sniper to fight another day is mission failure. First, the unit must find the sniper or sniper team. Techniques for detecting a sniper include identifying likely sniper locations, focusing observation on sniper movement, and seeking audible or visible signs. Backtracking, which integrates the following techniques in paragraphs 6-174 through 6-177, is useful for finding snipers. 

6-174. Identify likely insurgent sniper locations. An insurgent sniper is a line-of-sight asset. The larger the sniper’s kill zone, the closer or the higher the sniper position must be to cover it. Smaller sniper kill zones create a narrow, if not linear, line of sight. In such cases, the sniper always chooses a position that offers a line of sight (for example, a road or alley, inside a building, at an opening such as a window or doorway). 

6-175. Focus observation on sniper movement. Insurgent snipers typically plan infiltration and exfiltration routes. After identifying possible sniper locations, a unit commander focuses observation on these routes and denies a sniper the ability to reposition. Snipers operate slowly and with calculated movements to avoid detection. Detection of a sniper’s movement may not be easy. Units look for movement that does not fit into the environment. 

6-176. Seek audible or visible signs. Audible or visible indicators help locate insurgent snipers by sniper fires. Firing a weapon is a sniper’s greatest moment of risk; it offers the best opportunity to locate a sniper or sniper team. The acoustic, light, and heat signatures associated with the projection of a bullet from a sniper’s rifle are the greatest vulnerabilities. Infrared sensors can detect a muzzle’s flash out to 1 kilometer (0.6 miles). Acoustic sensors can detect a muzzle’s blast from several hundred meters to farther than 1 kilometer. Often, the muzzle flash and blast throw dust into the air. The bullet’s shock wave is a miniature sonic boom. This noise, caused by the bullet travelling at supersonic speed, is audible farther than 1 kilometer (0.6 miles) away. 

6-177. Backtrack sounds, sights, and angles. In a city, the backtracking process is complicated by buildings’ obstructing the view of the insurgent sniper’s position. Backtracking is challenging, but it is how Soldiers relate shot angles, kill zones, movement, and audible and visible signs to the sniper’s location. Experience and training make a major contribution to accurate backtracking. 

###### **Eliminate the Insurgent Sniper** 

6-178. Once spotted, the insurgent sniper must be killed or forced to surrender. To succeed in doing so, the unit must rapidly find, fix, and finish (destroy) or capture the active insurgent sniper. Paragraphs 6-179 through 6-182 provide useful techniques for eliminating insurgent snipers. 

###### **_Avoid the Kill Zone_** 

6-179. Soldiers figure out the insurgents’ kill zone and stay out of it. A unit may also want to eliminate or at least reduce the insurgents’ available targets. When a unit removes insurgent targets, it curtails insurgency mission success; the insurgent sniper will need to move or at least adjust position to remain effective. 

###### **_Move Rapidly_** 

6-180. When contact is made, on-scene commanders rapidly calculate the dispositions of their own forces, the quick reaction forces, and adjacent friendly forces and the factors in time and space considerations to determine how to neutralize threats. Because of the fleeting nature of snipers, it is often preferable for onscene commanders to begin to maneuver against hostile snipers with unengaged portions of their own forces rather than wait for quick reaction forces. 

###### **_Consider Sniper Hunting with Another Sniper_** 

6-181. Throughout history, many units, engaged in urban combat, have employed direct and indirect supporting arms, close air support, or large numbers of ground forces to counter urban snipers. However, the Russian and German forces of World War II found the best solution to a sniper threat to be the employment of their own snipers in a counter-sniper role. Advantages to using a trained sniper to counter enemy snipers include those following: 

- A sniper team has relative ease of movement over the urban battlespace compared to that of a larger ground formation. 

- Counter-snipers know the habitual methods of their enemy counterparts. 

- The ability to deliver precision fire results in a reduction in civilian and friendly casualties and collateral damage. 

###### **_Confirm the Enemy Sniper is Neutralized_** 

6-182. In this context, neutralization means the killing or capture of the sniper. A captured enemy sniper can be a valuable source of information. 

#### **COUNTERING DRIVE BY SHOOTINGS** 

6-183. A drive by shooting is the firing of small arms by vehicle occupants as the vehicle passes an area, followed by the vehicle’s immediate departure of the area. It is an effective technique for an insurgency because it allows rapid infiltration and exfiltration, requires little logistic support, has a chance of success, and has little chance of resulting in a decisive engagement. Any structure or location near a roadway is a target for a drive by shooting. Usual targets for drive by shootings are vulnerable, easily escapable locations. Attackers avoid well-defended locations. 

6-184. Establishing static checkpoints or closing roads near an area of heightened threat often prevents further drive by attacks along a specific avenue of approach. However, the insurgents are not eliminated, and they then seek new or different ways to attack. Timely and accurate reporting by subordinate units can allow higher HQ to integrate Army aviation (manned and unmanned) and/or organic or tasked echelon-specific UAS (to include firing) platforms to track vehicles after a drive by attack. Aerial surveillance enables COIN forces to target insurgents. 

6-185. One technique is to conduct mobile checkpoints. These can disrupt the ability of insurgents to transport weapons in vehicles. Random snap checkpoints may encourage drive by shooters to seek elsewhere for targets. 

#### **INFORMATION ACTIVITIES WITHIN DEFENSIVE TASKS** 

6-186. Information activities are deliberately integrated into defensive tasks to complement and reinforce the success of overall operations. The successful exploitation of violent insurgent tactics, harsh insurgent behavior toward the HN population, and failures of the insurgents to achieve their goals requires precise timing and coordination. Some units choose to prepare an information engagement plan and, thus, their readiness to provide an immediate response to insurgent attacks or propaganda. For example, they may plan to send a field grade officer to an insurgent attack site to talk to local media and thereby to disseminate the correct story. Such efforts may go far, along with reward or anonymity, toward influencing the populace to provide information that may break apart the insurgency’s networks. Information supplied specifically by the populace is critical in countering ambushes, IEDs, snipers, and drive by shootings by interrupting the insurgency’s decision-making cycle. (See paragraphs 4-48 through 4-65 for details on conducting information activities.) 

#### **ADDITIONAL PROTECTION CONSIDERATIONS FOR COUNTERINSURGENCY** 

6-187. Protection considerations are the same in concept between conventional operations and IW, specifically COIN operations. However, one aspect of a greater degree for COIN forces is their responsibility for protecting local civilians in their AOs. By securing the populace, COIN forces increase their effectiveness in all LOEs and gain allies who will provide information and cooperation from within specific LOEs. 

Information sharing serves to increase the security of those tactical units conducting COIN operations, as well as the local populace. Paragraphs 6-188 through 6-198 address protection considerations. 

##### **ANTITERRORISM MEASURES** 

6-188. One means for disrupting insurgent attack plans is to implement antiterrorism measures. These consistently change the look of a security posture to defeat surveillance attempts and introduce uncertainty to a site’s overall security plan, thereby making it difficult for the insurgency to predict friendly actions accurately. Examples of antiterrorism measures follow: 

- Moving prefabricated barriers, vehicular barriers, Class IV (construction materials) supplies, or objects in other supply classes to route traffic around base. 

- Starting random security patrols in the surrounding blocks. 

- Installing floodlights that operate at random times. 

- Changing guard shifts at random times. 

- Changing access times for entry points. 

- Changing access procedures at random. 

- Changing methods for searching personnel on a random basis. 

- Observing surrounding areas with crewed aircraft and UAS organic or tasked echelon specific platforms at random times. 

##### **SURVIVABILITY** 

6-189. Defensive operations typically demand the most effort and resources for survivability. Activities in the defense include constructing survivability positions for CP, artillery, air and missile defense, and critical equipment and supplies. Soldiers prepare individual and crew-served fighting positions and combat vehicle fighting positions. Survivability efforts must consider conventional threats (direct and indirect fires) and unconventional threats (suicide bombings, VBIEDs, CBRN hazards). The relative amount of survivability effort placed against these threats depends on the threat analysis and the available resources. Paragraphs 6-190 through 6-192 address additional survivability considerations. 

###### **Vehicle and Personnel Armor Protection** 

6-190. Vehicle and personnel armor protection saves lives and makes it more difficult for an insurgency to conduct a lethal attack. However, the added weight causes vehicles, especially the engine, to wear out much more quickly than normal. Individual body armor increases Soldier load and degrades maneuverability and endurance. Additional protection measures to make insurgent attacks more difficult include those following: 

- Hardening static sites to increase protection and to defeat or negate the effects of an attack. 

- Using natural or artificial materials to protect personnel, equipment, or facilities, such as those following: 

 - Concrete or expedient barriers. 

 - Sandbags, walls, shields, berms, or other types of physical protection. 

- Protecting resources from blast, direct and indirect fire, heat, radiation, or EAs. 

###### **Combat Identification** 

6-191. Combat identification is the process of attaining accurate and sufficient enough characterizations of detected objects in the OE to support an engagement decision. Rapid categorization of these objects as friendly, enemy, or neutral addresses their equal potential as targets. Combat identification ensures enemy forces can be destroyed, friendly entities can be identified and prevented from becoming fratricide victims, and neutral entities can be identified to prevent collateral damage. (See paragraph 5-126 for information on combat identification.) Common combat identification techniques include the use of the following: 

- Glint tape. 

- Infrared lights and strobes. 

- Heat sources. 

- VS-17 signal panels. 

- Flares. 

- Arm bands. 

###### **Insurgent Targeting** 

6-192. Individual and small groups of Soldiers, leaders, and civilians are targets for insurgents. This type of targeting is not only for lethal operations such as attacks against an individual but also for nonlethal operations such as kidnapping, subversion, or character attacks. Established individual protection measures remain the first line of defense. Basic site protection operations are a key building block to secure the populace. 

##### **CRITICAL SITE SECURITY (STATIC POSTS OR BASES)** 

6-193. Each static post or base requires a full-time detachment at the location of the vital asset. The size of the vital asset, the threat, and the distance to the nearest available reserve or response force determines the size of the detachment. Employing surveillance devices and intruder alarms satisfies the mandatory consideration for conserving labor. 

##### **OBSERVATION POSTS** 

6-194. An _observation post_ is a position from which observations are made or fires are directed and adjusted (FM 3-90). Although an observation post has too little combat power to secure a vital asset, it can immediately notify the asset or call for support. Also, leaders can incorporate Javelin command launch units and small UASs as surveillance tools (day or night), depending on the METT-TC (I) variables. (See ATP 3- 21.8 for information.) 

##### **VEHICLE PATROLS** 

6-195. Vehicle patrols are useful for providing periodic coverage to many low-categorized vital assets. Timings for patrols vary to prevent the likelihood of ambush and to retain the element of surprise. Patrols are strong enough to deal with anticipated threats, and they are supported by a local reserve. (See ATP 3-21.10 for information.) 

##### **DISMOUNTED PATROLS** 

6-196. Dismounted patrols provide periodic coverage to low-categorized vital assets. Foot patrols are particularly valuable at vital points of congested movement, difficult observation, and easily afforded concealment to insurgency forces, such as those in busy city blocks. (See paragraphs 5-219 through 5-259 for information on patrols and patrolling.) 

##### **SECURITY DURATIONS** 

6-197. Clearly articulating the durations of security operations allows security elements to establish associated time requirements that drive security operations planning. Examples are the method for establishing observation posts (either mounted or dismounted); battle positions; the length of crewed aircraft or UAS organic or tasked echelon-specific platform rotations, supplementary support to mounted or dismounted patrols, or service over extended distances; and the necessary logistic and communications support to execute the mission. 

6-198. Security durations are either short (shorter than 12 hours) or long (longer than 12 hours). Duration can also apply to depth, especially in an observation post, since proper deployment into an area to achieve the requisite coverage in the security objective area takes time. Commanders and subordinate leaders consider tasks, commander’s critical information requirements (CCIRs), the latest time information is of value, tactical risk, movement techniques, reconnaissance methods, and formations when articulating the security duration. 

**_Note_** : Observation posts, vehicle patrols, dismounted patrols, and security durations enable local security. 

This page intentionally left blank. 

##### **Chapter 7** 

### **Stability Considerations in Counterinsurgency** 

The requirement for military formations to conduct stability-focused operations is not new. Section I covers the doctrinal foundation, stability environment, and Army’s six stability operations tasks for operations focused on the stability element of combined arms operations. Sections II and III focus on the challenges confronting commanders, staffs, and subordinate leaders in accomplishing stability-focused missions or tasks, specifically area security operations and security force assistance (SFA). 

**_Notes_ .** The involvement of the U.S. Army in military conflict from the Revolutionary War to Operation Enduring Freedom comprises eleven conventional military operations. Conversely, that same military history reveals hundreds of stability-focused operations, with recent history proving no different. Since the fall of the Berlin Wall, the United States led or participated in over fifteen operations in places such as Haiti, Liberia, Somalia, the Balkans, Iraq, and Afghanistan. While the magnitude of violence may not match conventional operations, history often measures the duration of stability operations in decades. This fact, combined with the disturbing spread of international terrorism, the number of fragile states affording safe haven to terrorist organizations or possessing weapons of mass destruction (WMD), and the endless array of humanitarian and natural disasters, illustrates the increasing requirement for stability-focused operations. 

Military formations conduct stability-focused operations to transition the security and governance of the populace to legitimate civilian authorities. The brigade combat team (BCT) lacks the organic capability to stabilize an assigned area of operations (AO) independently. Its central role in those counterinsurgency (COIN) operations focused on stability is to establish and maintain unity of effort toward achieving the operation’s political objectives. To do this, it employs combined arms formations that execute offensive and defensive operations and stability operations tasks to identify and mitigate critical sources of instability. Essentially, the BCT unifies military operations with the activities of government agencies, nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), and elements of the private sector to seize, retain, and exploit the initiative and to consolidate gains. 

##### **SECTION I – STABILITY OPERATIONS OVERVIEW** 

7-1. Stability ultimately aims to establish conditions the local populace regards as legitimate, acceptable, and predictable. Stabilization is a process in which personnel identify and mitigate underlying sources of instability to establish the conditions for long-term stability. Stability operations tasks focus on identifying and targeting the root causes of instability and building the capacity of local institutions. COIN forces accomplish stability missions and perform tasks across the range of military operations in coordination with (ICW) other instruments of national power. Stability missions and tasks are part of broader efforts to establish and maintain the conditions for stability in an unstable area before or during hostilities or to reestablish enduring peace and stability after open hostilities cease. 

#### **FUNDAMENTALS OF STABILIZATION** 

7-2. COIN forces apply the fundamentals of stabilization to offense, defense, and stability-focused operations to achieve political and military objectives. (See ADP 3-07 and FM 3-24 for information on the fundamentals of stabilization.) The following fundamentals of stabilization lay the foundation for long-term stability: 

- Conflict transformation. 

- Unity of effort. 

- Increased host nation (HN) capacity and capabilities. 

- HN ownership and public perception of the HN government’s legitimacy. 

##### **CONFLICT TRANSFORMATION** 

7-3. Conflict transformation is the process of converting the actors and conditions that motivate violent conflict into a governmental process to address the causes of instability. It sets the HN on a sustainable, positive trajectory along which transformational processes directly address the dynamics causing instability. The employment of COIN forces in a combat role serves as a temporary solution until the situation is stabilized and HN forces are able to provide security for the populace. In all cases, the combat role supports the HN’s ability to provide for its internal security and external defense. 

##### **UNITY OF EFFORT** 

7-4. COIN operations typically demand unity of command. The challenge for military and civilian leaders is to forge unity of effort or unity of purpose among the diverse array of actors involved in a stability-focused operation. Achieving such a state is the essence of _unified action_ —the synchronization, coordination, or integration of the activities of governmental and nongovernmental entities with military operations to achieve unity of effort (JP 1, Volume 1). Unity of effort (see paragraphs 3-13 through 3-15) is fundamental to successful incorporation of all the instruments of national power into a collaborative approach when conducting stability operations tasks during military operations. 

7-5. When countering insurgency, one example of unity of effort is a military commander and a civilian leader ensuring the governance and economic lines of effort (LOEs) are fully coordinated with military operations. Unity of effort among nationally, culturally, and organizationally distinct partners is difficult to maintain, given their different layers of command. Achieving unity of effort requires participants to overcome cultural barriers and to set aside parochial agendas. It also requires each organization’s understanding of the capabilities and limitations of the others. 

##### **HOST NATION CAPACITY AND CAPABILITIES** 

7-6. Building HN capacity and capabilities is the outcome of comprehensive interorganizational activities, programs, and military-to-military engagements enhancing partners’ abilities to establish security, governance, economic development, essential services, rule of law, and other critical government functions. The institutional force advises and trains partner army activities on building institutional capacity for professional education and force generation and sustainment. The Army integrates the capabilities of the operating forces and the institutional force to support interorganizational efforts toward building capacity and capabilities, primarily through security cooperation (SC) (see paragraph 7-195) interactions. COIN forces apply a comprehensive approach (see paragraphs 7-14 through 7-16) toward sustained engagement with foreign and domestic partners to codevelop mutually beneficial capacities and capabilities and to address shared interests. 

7-7. Unified action is an indispensable feature of building HN capacity and capabilities. In operations characterized by stability operations tasks, unified action to enhance partners’ abilities to establish security, governance, economic development, essential services, rule of law, and other critical government functions exemplifies the building of HN capacity and capabilities. During SFA (see section III), the primary focus of security force assistance brigades (SFABs) is normally building the capacity and capabilities of foreign security forces (FSF) and their supporting institutions. On occasion, the unit as a whole or select units of the unit (for example, the BCT) may support SFA activities. SFA encompasses various activities related to the organizing, equipping, training, advising, and assessing of FSF and their supporting institutions. SFA activities that SFABs and BCTs conduct build HN capacity and capabilities to defend against internal, external, and transnational threats to stability. (See FM 3-22 for information on building HN capacity and capabilities.) 

##### **HOST NATION OWNERSHIP AND HOST NATION GOVERNMENT LEGITIMACY** 

7-8. Ownership and legitimacy are conditions rooted in specific audiences’ perceptions of the legality and morality of a set of actions and of the propriety of the individual or organizational authorities in taking those actions. Legitimacy enables HN ownership by building public trust and confidence. Ownership and legitimacy affect every aspect of operations from every conceivable perspective. The HN government’s legitimacy and ownership of the mission enable successful operations characterized by stability operations tasks. 

**_Note_ .** _Security sector reform_ involves a comprehensive set of programs and activities undertaken by a host nation to improve the way it provides safety, security, and justice (JP 3-07). Security sector reform may be an activity conducted during SC (see paragraph 7-195). 

7-9. The COIN force’s primary role in security sector reform is to support the reformation, restructuring, or reestablishment of the armed forces and the defense sector across the range of military operations. The overall objective is to support in a way that promotes an effective and legitimate HN government and its ownership of the mission and that is transparent, accountable, and responsive to civilian authority. (See ADP 3-07 for information HN ownership and HN government legitimacy.) 

#### **STABILIZATION FRAMEWORK** 

7-10. A stabilization framework, based on conditions in the AO, of initial response, transformation, and sustainability fostering helps COIN forces determine the requisite training and task organization of forces before initial deployment and serves as a guide to actions in an operation focused on stability operations tasks. A force deployed into an AO with a nonexistent local government may conduct a set of tasks while another force may conduct another set of tasks in an AO with a functioning local government. Paragraphs 7-11 through 7-13 describe the three phases that facilitate the identification of lead responsibilities and the determination of priorities. (See FM 3-07 for information on the stabilization framework.) 

##### **INITIAL RESPONSE PHASE IN STABILIZATION** 

7-11. Initial response actions generally reflect the activity executed to stabilize a crisis state in the AO. COIN forces typically perform initial response actions during or directly after a conflict or disaster in which the security situation prohibits the introduction of civilian personnel. Initial response actions aim to provide a secure environment in which relief forces can attend to the immediate, local humanitarian needs. They reduce the level of violence and human suffering while creating conditions that enable other actors to participate safely in relief efforts. 

##### **TRANSFORMATION PHASE IN STABILIZATION** 

7-12. Stabilization, reconstruction, and capacity building are transformation actions performed in a relatively secure environment. Transformation actions occur either in crisis or in vulnerable states. These actions aim to build HN capacity across multiple sectors. They are essential to the continuing stability of the environment and foster sustainability in the COIN’s AO. 

##### **SUSTAINABILITY FOSTERING PHASE IN STABILIZATION** 

7-13. Actions that foster sustainability encompass long-term efforts that capitalize on capacity building and reconstruction. Their successful accomplishment establishes conditions that enable sustainable development. Usually, military forces perform sustainability fostering only when the security environment is stable enough to implement the long-term programs committed to the viability of the institutions and economy of the HN. Often military forces conduct these long-term efforts to support broader, civilian-led efforts. 

#### **COMPREHENSIVE APPROACH IN STABILIZATION** 

7-14. A comprehensive approach toward achieving unity of effort during stability operations tasks requires contributions from a variety of partners outside the United States and the U.S. Government. These partners include foreign military and police forces, NGOs, international organizations, HN organizations, news media, and businesses. Many partners have no formal relationship with U.S. Army units but are, nevertheless, instrumental in achieving the desired outcomes. COIN units interact with these partners effectively to exchange information and strive for unified action. COIN units demonstrate to the HN and international community through action their character, competence, and commitment to adhering to and upholding the Army Ethic.

7-15. When developing an operational approach, commanders consider methods to employ a combination of defeat mechanisms and stability mechanisms (see paragraphs 4-77 through 4-82). Defeat mechanisms relate to offensive and defensive operations (see chapters 5 and 6). Stability mechanisms relate to stability operations tasks, security, and consolidating gains in an AO. Planning operations related to stability mechanisms employed by the COIN force require a comprehensive approach, as well as an in-depth understanding of the stability environment (see paragraph 7-17). Planning nests within policy, internal defense and development (IDAD) strategy, the campaign plan, and any other higher echelon plans. Continuous and open to change, planning includes identifying how best to assist the FSF and developing a sequence of actions to change the situation. Planning also involves anticipating consequences of actions and developing ways to mitigate those and thereby to attain conditions that engender lasting, stable peace. 

**_Note_ .** IDAD focuses on building viable institutions (political, economic, social, and military) that respond to societal needs. Ideally, IDAD is a preemptive strategy. However, when an insurgency or other threat develops, IDAD becomes an active strategy to combat that threat. To support the HN effectively, U.S. Forces, especially planners, consider the HN’s IDAD strategy. 

7-16. Considering the elements of operational art (the cognitive [conceptual in nature] approach by commanders and staffs—supported by their skills, knowledge, experiences, creativity, and judgments [see ADP 3-0]) provides the commander and staff with a combination of conventional forces while leveraging the unique capabilities of special operations forces to assist in achieving stability-focused operations. Planning for and selecting the appropriate mix of military forces, the Expeditionary Civilian Workforce, civilian personnel, and contractors are deliberate decisions based on thorough mission analysis and a pairing of available capabilities to requirements. Important considerations in these decisions include the nature of the HN force, the skills and competencies required by the HN force, and the situation and environment into which the COIN force will deploy. 

#### **STABILITY ENVIRONMENT** 

7-17. Stability-focused operations range across all military operations and offer perhaps the most diverse set of circumstances the COIN faces. The objectives of stability-focused operations are conditions regarded as acceptable by the local populace in terms of violence; functioning government, economic, and societal institutions; and adherence to local laws, rules, and norms of behavior. During unified land operations, the COIN provides the means for seizing and retaining initiative through its partnership with associated enabling organizations better suited for bringing stability to the operational environment (OE). To seize, retain, and exploit the initiative and to consolidate gains in stability-focused operations, the COIN identifies and mitigates sources of instability, understands and nests operations within political objectives, and achieves unity of effort across diverse organizations. 

##### **IDENTIFYING SOURCES OF INSTABILITY** 

7-18. The COIN conducts information collection to gain a detailed understanding of the sources of instability and the capabilities and intentions of key actors in its AO. Sources of instability are actors, actions, or conditions that exceed the legitimate authority’s capacity to exercise effective governance, maintain civil control, and ensure economic development. The insurgency leverages sources of instability to create conflict, exacerbate existing conditions, or threaten to collapse failing or recovering states. Examples of sources of instability follow: 

- Ungoverned areas. 

- Religious, ethnic, economic, and political differences among the local populace. 

- Natural disasters. 

- Resource scarcity. 

- Individuals disrupting legitimate governance. 

- Degraded infrastructure. 

- Economic strife. 

- Immature, undeveloped, or atrophied systems. 

- Ineffective or corrupt host-nation security forces (HNSF). 

7-19. Commanders and staffs apply the same fundamental planning processes in the military decision-making process (MDMP) and the integrating processes—intelligence preparation of the operational environment (IPOE) process to identify the tactical problem. They conduct information collection to fulfill priority intelligence requirements (PIRs) or to fill identified information gaps. Commanders and staffs use three additional integrating processes: targeting (see chapter 4, section IV); risk management (RM) (see paragraph 4-16); and knowledge management (see paragraph 4-10). When identifying sources of instability, commanders and staffs find assistance in critical thinking, innovative problem-solving, and leveraging different tools to address these tactical problems. Thorough analysis, local leader interviews, public engagement, unified action partner leverage, and research are standard methods for identifying sources of instability. Commanders and staffs consider operational variables (ICW division and corps staffs) and the variables of METT-TC (I), which stands for mission, enemy, terrain and weather, troops and support available, time available, civil considerations, and informational considerations—with an emphasis on civil considerations, to deepen their understanding of the interests and motivations particular to different groups and individuals and to enhance their situational understanding. 

7-20. Interactions of various actors affect the COIN’s OE in terms of operational variables and the METT-TC (I) variables. Some of these actors include those following: 

- Unified action partners. 

- NGOs. 

- Private volunteer organizations. 

- International and private security organizations. 

- Media. 

- Multinational corporations. 

- Transnational criminal organizations. 

- Insurgents. 

- Violent extremist organizations. 

- Tribes, clans, and ethnic groups native to the AO. 

- Regional influences such as other nation-states. 

7-21. Commanders and staffs consider alternative perspectives and approaches to those used in offense and defense. COIN forces analyze sources of instability from local public perspective and from the U.S. military’s perspective to understand the differences between the viewpoints. During the IPOE, the COIN force identifies key actors and their interests or agendas. Additionally, the force analyzes how these key actors influence the local civil capacity; this analysis drives the force’s planning effort for the accomplishment of stability operations tasks. Staffs conduct preparation with the aim to understand the unique aspects of stability-focused operations. For example, at the BCT level, the brigade assistant engineer might assess the local electrical grid system of an assigned AO, or the brigade surgeon or medical planner might assess HN medical facilities and their capacity before employment in an assigned AO. This staff-specific assessment further enables the conduct of the six stability operations tasks (see paragraphs 7-47 through 7-49) and renders the BCT’s planning effort during stability-focused operations more informed and efficient. 

7-22. Once commanders and staffs understand the OE, the COIN force applies a mixture of stability mechanisms (see paragraph 4-76) to set conditions to retain and exploit stabilizing factors. A stability mechanism is the primary method through which friendly forces affect civilians to attain conditions that engender lasting, stable peace. Stability mechanisms relate to stability operations, security, and consolidating gains in an AO. The four stability mechanisms are to compel, control, influence, and support. Combinations of stability mechanisms produce complementary and reinforcing outcomes that accomplish the mission more effectively and efficiently than single mechanisms alone. 

7-23. COIN forces simultaneously use stability mechanisms such as compel and control to seize initiative. To compel is to use or threaten to use lethal force to establish control and dominance, to effect behavioral change, or to enforce compliance with mandates, agreements, or civil authority. To control is to impose civil order. Offensive operations reveal and exploit enemy weaknesses by defeating, destroying, or neutralizing threat forces. These actions disrupt threat forces, prevent them from negatively influencing populations, and provide opportunities to continue exploiting weaknesses, but they are not decisive by themselves. In designing these actions, COIN forces consider how they will compel the population, what they will compel them to do, and whether the action will result in positive, neutral, or negative public support in the long and short terms. (See FM 3-96 for information on the MDMP and the integrating processes.)

##### **UNDERSTANDING POLITICAL OBJECTIVES** 

7-24. Political objectives frame the unique operations necessary for conducting stability operations. General political objectives are broad and conceptual in nature, but they offer contextual guidance that informs the expanded purpose of the echelons above the COIN commander’s intent. They may shift and change as the OE changes. That same guidance unifies or alienates partners who may fall outside the military chain of command. 

7-25. Given the inherently complex and uncertain nature of political objectives, the commander and staff use the Army design methodology (see chapter 4) to determine the root cause of instability and approaches to solve problems. The Army design methodology entails framing an OE, framing the problem, and developing an operational approach toward solving the problem. It results in an improved understanding of an OE. From this improved understanding, the commander issues planning guidance, including an operational approach, for more detailed planning using the MDMP (see chapter 4). 

7-26. Incorporating political objectives into the planning process (see chapter 4) is a shared task among the COIN staff members. For an assigned stability-focused operation, each staff officer understands the general and specific political objectives and the commander’s intent two levels up. They consider the implications and effects of those political objectives when presenting the commander with running estimates, courses of action (COAs), and other decision support staff products. The staff understands how to communicate general and specific political objectives into the themes and messages delivered in the operation order (OPORD) and fragmentary orders (FRAGORDs) that Soldiers are to display through their actions. These political objectives must translate across the entirety of the OE yet be understood by subordinate units, allowing the units to shape public perception. 

##### **ACHIEVING UNITY OF EFFORT ACROSS DIVERSE ORGANIZATIONS** 

7-27. COIN commanders and staffs understand how to build relationships with many diverse organizations in their AOs. These relationships allow the COIN force to nest operations with both their higher headquarters (HQ) and the overall U.S. effort in the joint operational area. A whole-of-government approach in collaboration and cooperation with unified action partners (see paragraph 3-13) is the key component of stability-focused operations. The staff incorporates personnel from these organizations into the operations process as soon as possible. 

7-28. By building relationships, COIN forces reinforce the COIN operation’s legitimacy. Legitimacy is of great importance to stability operations. Military activities sustain the operation’s and the local emerging or HN government’s legitimacy. Having a just cause and earning and sustaining trust affect several relationships: trust with U.S. residents; trust within the unified force; trust with allies, government organizations, NGOs, and coalition partners; trust with the HN government; and trust with HN citizens. Restraint through the disciplined, ethical application of lethal force significantly influences those trust relationships and the operation’s legitimacy. A direct relationship exists between restraint, the protection of noncombatant civilians, and legitimacy in any military operation, especially in stability operations. 

###### **Military Police** 

7-29. Mission-tailored military police support to COIN forces integrates police intelligence operations (see ATP 3-39.20 regarding police intelligence operations) throughout offensive, defensive, and stability-focused operations. Police intelligence operations address the reality that, in some OEs, the threat is more criminal than conventional in nature. In those environments, it is not uncommon for members of armed groups, insurgents, and other belligerents to use or mimic established criminal networks, activities, and practices to move contraband, raise funds, or further their goals and objectives. Police intelligence can provide relevant, actionable police information or police intelligence to COIN forces for integration into the operations process and fusion with other intelligence data. The Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division and provost marshal staffs provide police intelligence to COIN commanders and staffs that identifies indicators of potential crimes and criminal threats against facilities or personnel.

###### **Special Operations Forces** 

7-30. During COIN operations, the BCT typically coordinates with a special operations task force or a joint special operations task force. Army special operations forces operating in a BCT’s AO coordinate their activities with the BCT regardless of command or supporting relationships. To best support integration efforts and to generate and sustain interdependence, the BCT and the special operations unit exchange a variety of liaison and coordination elements. Doing so for the intelligence and fires warfighting functions is especially important. These range in size from individual liaisons to small coordination elements. Whatever their size or location, these elements coordinate, synchronize, and deconflict missions in the other unit’s AO. Exchanging liaisons creates conditions that foster interdependence. The exercise of interdependence facilitates shared understanding between the BCT and special operations forces and provides a conduit by which the two units can provide each other relevant, useful, and timely information during the operations processes. Liaisons attend and participate in all planning efforts, update briefs, and working groups. (See ADP 3-05 for information on special operations forces.) 

7-31. Civil affairs operations (CAO) are essential to the conduct of stability-focused operations. The full capability of the civil affairs (CA) force manifests in the conduct of stability operations tasks in every environment across the range of military operations. CA support to stability operations tasks includes the execution of all five CA core tasks, employment of CA functional specialists, and continuous analysis of the civil component of the OE in terms of both operational and mission variables by CA staff elements. CA activities are civil reconnaissance, civil engagement, civil-military operations center (CMOC), civil information management, and CAO staff support. CA forces also conduct military government operations— including transitional military authority and support to civil administration—and provide support to CA-supported activities such as populace and resources control (PRC), foreign humanitarian aid, and civil foreign assistance. 

7-32. CA support to stability-focused operations depends on the nature of the operation and the condition of the affected civilian population and institutions. The CA staff continually monitors the condition of the HN throughout the operation, applies available resources to affect the civilian population, and recommends the necessary functional skills for supporting this critical phase of the operation. CA supports the BCT, U.S. Government agencies, and HN civil administration in transitioning power back to the local government. During the transition from offensive or defensive to stability-focused operations, CA units place greater emphasis on infrastructure, economic stability, and governance expertise. (See FM 3-57 for information on CA.) 

###### **Provincial Reconstruction Teams** 

7-33. A provincial reconstruction team can be a valuable part of a long-term strategy to transition the functions of security, governance, and economy to provincial governments. It is a potential combat multiplier for maneuver commanders performing governance and economy functions and providing expertise to programs designed to strengthen infrastructure and the institutions of local governments. A provincial reconstruction team leverages the principles of reconstruction and development to build HN capacity while speeding the transition of security, justice, and economic development to the control of the HN. Depending on the situation, a provincial reconstruction team retains between 60 to 90 personnel members. It may employ the following complement of personnel: 

- Provincial reconstruction team leader. 

- Deputy team leader. 

- Multinational force liaison officer. 

- Rule of law coordinator. 

- Provincial action officer. 

- Public diplomacy officer. 

- Agricultural advisor. 

- • Engineer. 

- Development officer. 

- Governance team. 

- CA team. 

- Bilingual cultural advisor. 

###### **Intergovernmental and Nongovernmental Organizations** 

7-34. COIN forces recognize the value of intergovernmental and NGOs and build effective relationships with these actors. These organizations may have the most extensive amounts of resources to conduct stability operations tasks in the COIN’s AO. Intergovernmental organizations and NGOs are the primary sources of subject matter expertise in many essential services and governance topics. They are also the primary provider of humanitarian, infrastructure, and essential services in immature OEs. They often have experienced and detailed knowledge of the civil environment. Usually, they have a better understanding of the civil considerations than any other actors besides HN personnel. Their insight can assist the COIN force in the continual processes of developing understanding of and shaping the environment. 

7-35. Building relationships with intergovernmental organizations and NGOs is unique, as opposed to doing so with HN forces and interagency actors who often have different mandates and alternative perspectives to stability-focused operations. COIN commanders and staffs utilize these differences to see the OE and tactical problems from different perspectives. Additionally, understanding where intergovernmental organizations and NGOs are in the AO and the nature of their activities helps develop a common operational picture (COP). This COP enables the COIN force to anticipate changes to the OE, the effects of intergovernmental organizations and NGOs on stability operations tasks and COIN operations, and future friction points between the organization’s and the COIN’s interests. 

7-36. Building relationships with intergovernmental organizations and NGOs is sometimes difficult because these organizations are reluctant to establish associations with U.S. Forces. The COIN force remains cognizant of this and establishes these relationships on benefits to all involved parties. Intergovernmental organizations and NGOs bring valuable resources, information regarding the civilian population and the OE, and alternative perspectives to the COIN operation. Examples of interagency personnel capable of providing valuable information to COIN forces are U.S. embassy’s country team members, chiefs of stations or bases, defense attachés, and subject matter experts from other Government departments (for example, the Departments of Agriculture, Justice, or the Treasury). 

7-37. Humanitarian organizations avoid any blurring of the distinction between neutral, independent, and impartial humanitarian and developmental aid derived from political engagement, as the latter is potentially linked to security concerns or biased support. The COIN force often works through civilian representatives from the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), United Nations, or HN when coordinating with NGOs. The force avoids publicly citing NGOs as information sources since that might jeopardize their neutrality and invite retaliation by adversaries. COIN forces primarily use CMOCs operated by CA units to coordinate with NGOs. (See ATP 3-07.5 for information on intergovernmental organizations and NGOs.) COIN forces operating with NGOs follow these guidelines: 

- Military personnel wear uniforms when conducting relief activities. 

- Military personnel make prior arrangements before visiting NGOs. 

- Military personnel do not refer to NGOs as force multipliers or partners or other similar terms. 

- U.S. Forces respect an NGO’s decision not to serve as an implementing partner. 

##### **SEIZING THE INITIATIVE** 

7-38. The enduring theme of seizing the initiative is as applicable in stability-focused operations as in offensive and defensive operations. The significant difference is the context in which the operational framework occurs. Stability-focused operations have fewer specific applications of tactics and procedures. The COIN commander requires study, critical thinking, and creativity to address the tactical problems in a complex environment. Stability-focused operations have broader temporal considerations; this operational framework occurs before, during, and after conflict, as well as simultaneously with offensive and defensive operations. The commander considers the effects of the temporal aspect and manages them appropriately. 

7-39. Stability-focused operations are conceptual by nature. The COIN commander develops understanding of how each action affects the other elements in the complex system of HN government institutions, civil society, and local economies. Success in seizing the initiative from a stability-focused perspective is critical in preventing conflict, setting conditions for success during the offense and defense, and securing hard-won successes in a post-conflict environment. 

##### **RETAINING THE INITIATIVE** 

7-40. Retaining initiative gained through the offensive and stability-focused operations requires the COIN to anticipate and act on civil requirements while actively averting threat actions. Shaping public perception to recognize the civil authority’s legitimacy is critical in retaining the initiative. In many circumstances, security is the most influential element affecting the population beyond their basic needs of food, water, and shelter. A secure environment fosters a functioning economy, which provides employment and gradually transfers the population’s dependence from military to civilian authorities and HN governments. 

7-41. COIN forces execute defensive and stability-focused operations to retain key terrain, guard populations, and protect critical capabilities that inhibit threat actions while fostering conditions to increase the impact of stabilizing efforts. Often, the COIN commander assigns these tasks as an economy of force to conduct offensive operations and those focused on stability operations tasks. These tasks take form in such actions as partnership with other domestic security forces but are executed to prevent instability. The objective is the public perception of the level of security as promoting evolving and often sequential growth and stabilization. HN actors are often the best and most informed sources on the local environment. 

##### **Example of an Economy of Force Battle** 

<mark>The 1st Battalion, 35th Armor (Task Force Conqueror), fought an economy of force mission for most of the Battle of Ramadi during the summer and fall of 2006. . . . Through a combination of partnering with Iraqi Security Forces (also called ISF), tribal engagement, aggressive Iraqi Police recruiting, and targeted U.S.-led operations, the task force was able to—</mark> 

- <mark>Reestablish the Iraqi Police in Ramadi.</mark> 

- <mark>Increase the capability of our partnered Iraqi Army battalion.</mark> 

<mark>• Link the sheiks of Anbar with the government of Iraq fostering the Anbar Awakening. The Battle of Ramadi had a clear beginning but no clear-cut end, and it was a battle fought on two main fronts. The first front was an incredibly lethal fight to wrest control of Ramadi back from Al-Qaeda; the second was a battle to link the population with the government of Iraq. In the end, it was a victory for the Soldiers, Sailors, Airmen, and Marines of the 1st Brigade, 1st Armored Division (Ready First Combat Team). The battle proved to be a blueprint for the emerging counterinsurgency doctrine, U.S. Army and Marine Corps Field Manual (FM) 3-24, [2006 version (obsolete),] which was being developed at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. While many of the actions of the Ready First now seem like simple application of doctrine, at the time, the following concepts ran counter to the prevailing conventional wisdom:</mark> 

- <mark>Living in small combat outposts.</mark> 

- <mark>Focusing on protecting the population.</mark> 

- <mark>Investing in the Iraqi Security Forces.</mark> 

- Working with tribal leaders. 

##### **EXPLOITING THE INITIATIVE** 

7-42. A secure OE enables unified action partners to capitalize on their unique capabilities, thus exploiting the initiative gained in earlier operations. Government agencies, NGOs, and other actors remain unified in purpose to maintain the effect. Effective civilian-military teaming starts with the development of shared goals, aims, and objectives and unity of purpose and leads to a relationship of shared trust and unity of effort. 

The COIN commander’s responsibilities include creating and fostering this dynamic and culture among organizations. 

7-43. Unity of effort is more than shared work across U.S. Government agencies. A COIN force works with multivarious HN actors (for example, political leaders, government agencies, security forces, local businesses) during stability-focused operations. The COIN leverages relationships with HN actors to deepen understanding of the information environment and to answer information requirements. 

7-44. HN and interagency personnel may not be the only actors among the unified action partners. The COIN’s AO may include allied and multinational forces. Understanding other forces’ capabilities, constraints and limitations, and command relationships facilitates mission preparation and execution of operations in a constantly changing OE. COIN forces cannot conduct successful stability-focused operations without building relationships. Each actor brings expertise, perspective, resources, and capabilities necessary for accomplishing stability operations tasks and achieving the desired end state for the overall operation. 

##### **STABILIZING THE ENVIRONMENT** 

7-45. Stability-focused operations seek to stabilize the environment enough for the HN to begin resolving the root causes of conflict and state failure. During consolidation of gains, these operations focus on security and stability operations tasks to establish conditions that support transition to legitimate authorities. Initially, the minimum performance of essential stability operations tasks provides security, food, water, shelter, and basic medical treatment. Once conditions allow, these tasks become the legal responsibility of U.S. Army forces. However, the commander may not need to have the COIN force conduct all these essential tasks. Other military units or appropriate civilian organizations may be available to perform these tasks adequately. As the OE and time allow and as appropriate, the effort involves the more deliberate execution of the six stability operations tasks within the COIN force’s LOEs. Within the shape-clear-hold-build-transition framework (see paragraphs 3-117 through 3-150), each phase addresses the stability operations tasks at differing degrees since LOEs vary within the framework. 

#### **STABILITY OPERATIONS** 

7-46. A _stability operation_ is an operation conducted outside the United States in coordination with other instruments of national power to establish or maintain a secure environment and provide essential governmental services, emergency infrastructure reconstruction, and humanitarian relief (ADP 3-0). COIN forces (for example, the BCT) execute operations focused on stability operations tasks against destabilizing factors by establishing unity of effort among diverse organizations. It then task-organizes and partners with other elements to mitigate sources of instability. (See ADP 3-0, ADP 3-07, FM 3-07, and ATP 3-07.5 for information on stability operations.) 

##### **SIX STABILITY OPERATIONS TASKS** 

7-47. U.S. Army forces often seek to stabilize their AOs by performing stability operations tasks. A single action taken by a U.S. COIN force or partner element can support multiple stability operations tasks because they are interrelated and interdependent. Each stability operations task carries unique considerations, but actions taken affect each differently. The COIN force plans, prepares, executes, and assesses operations to categorize impacts on its AO as positive, negative, or neutral, as regards both long-term and short-term effects. In stability-focused operations, planning and assessment require significant analyses supported by information collection activities (see paragraphs 4-162 through 4-166). These activities focus on identifiable indicators inside or outside the COIN force’s AO. To plan for the next operation, the COIN commander considers each stability operations task LOE within the context of the stability principles, and the staff analyzes measures of performance (MOPs) and measures of effectiveness (MOEs) during assessment (see paragraphs 3-53 and 4-11 through 4-15). Together, they are asking what is needed to accomplish the intended outcome. The Army’s six stability operations tasks are to— 

- Establish civil security. 

- Conduct SC. 

- Provide support to civil control. 

- Restore essential services. 

- Provide support to governance. 

- Provide support to economic and infrastructure development. 

7-48. The combination of stability operations tasks conducted during operations depends on the situation. In some operations, the HN can meet most of or all public requirements. In those cases, Army COIN forces work with and through HN authorities. Commanders employ CAOs to mitigate how the military presence affects the population and vice versa. Conversely, Army forces operating in a failed state may need to support public well-being. That situation requires Army forces to work with civilian organizations to restore basic capabilities. CAOs are essential for establishing the trust between Army forces and civilian organizations necessary for effective, working relationships. 

7-49. Six Army stability operations tasks (see figure 7-1) correspond directly to six joint stability functions. The tasks directly support the broader efforts within the joint stability functions. Together, the tasks and joint stability functions provide a mechanism for interagency tactical integration, linking the execution of discrete tasks to the requisite instruments of national power for establishing the end state conditions that would define success. Tasks performed in one function inevitably create related effects in another function. When planned and performed appropriately, carefully sequenced activities complement and reinforce those effects. The subordinate tasks performed by the BCT under the six stability operations tasks directly support the broader efforts executed as part of joint stabilization activities. 

**Figure 7-1. Mechanism for interagency tactical integration** 

7-50. Over time, to sustain safety and security, unified action partners perform numerous tasks across all joint stability functions. As part of a joint team with these partners, the BCT often performs related tasks among the six stability operations tasks to achieve a specific objective or set certain conditions. An example is the necessary effort to provide a safe, secure environment for the local populace. Compared to the outcomes of a single task focused on a local populace, safety and security are broad effects. The BCT helps achieve them by performing related tasks that assist in ending hostilities, isolating belligerent or criminal elements, demobilizing armed groups, eliminating explosives and other hazards, and providing public order and safety. 

##### **ESTABLISH CIVIL SECURITY** 

7-51. Civil security provides for the safety of the HN population, including protection from internal and external threats. The BCT coordinates operations to restore order, to halt violence, and to support, reinstate, or create civil authority by establishing a safe, secure, and stable environment for the local populace supporting the overall stability operation. (See ATP 3-07.5 for information on civil security.) Subtasks for establishing civil security include those following: 

- Enforcing the cessation of hostilities, peace agreements, and other arrangements. 

- Determining the dispositions and compositions of HN armed and intelligence services. 

- Conducting disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration. 

- Conducting border control, boundary security, and freedom of movement. 

- Supporting identification programs. 

- Protecting key personnel and facilities. 

- Clearing explosive and other hazards. 

###### **Task Organization and Actions to Establish Civil Security** 

7-52. The BCT conducts operations that directly support subtasks—enforce cessation of hostilities, peace agreements, and other arrangements; conduct border control, boundary security, and freedom of movement; support identification; and protect key personnel and facilities. It has limited capability to support, to determine the dispositions and compositions of national armed and intelligence services, to conduct disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration, and to clear explosives and other hazards. The stabilization framework—initial response, transformation, and sustainability fostering—enables the BCT to determine the requisite task organization and actions to create a safe, secure, and stable environment. 

###### **_Initial Response—Establish Civil Security_** 

7-53. During the initial response phase, the BCT often executes subordinate tasks because the HN lacks the capability. BCT subordinate units occupy their AOs in accordance with (IAW) geographical, political, socioeconomic, task, or supported actor boundary considerations. Information collection activities further support the development of understanding of the boundaries, requiring the BCT to shift unit assets and resources to better align with unified action partners and to mitigate sources of instability. BCTs may need to identify, segregate, search, and safeguard combatants and noncombatants and to move them out of the immediate AO. The BCT commander establishes priorities for the protection of civilian and military personnel, facilities, installations, and key terrain in the AO and initiates the stability principles of conflict transformation, unity of effort, and the building of partner capacity during the initial response. 

7-54. The BCT conducts operations that safeguard the local populace and prevent factions or actors from contributing to sources of instability. Ultimately, these operations convince rival factions and actors to secure their interests through negotiation and peaceful political processes rather than violence, intimidation, coercion, or corruption. BCT units are to remain neutral during this period. Supporting one or more factions or leveraging one faction against another can contribute to instability. The ideal local public perception views U.S. Forces as neutral, seeking public interests, providing security to the area, and allowing for further development. 

7-55. Identifying actors and their intentions during this phase through information collection allows the BCT to seize the initiative. The BCT commander and subordinate leaders reach, through engagements, binding agreements, and understandings with unified action partners, a determination of the best way to divide labor and to deconflict efforts, so partners are not working redundantly. Actor agendas or intents are not known or understood in their entirety during this phase. Psychological operations (PSYOP) staff planners and intelligence staff sections develop indicators that commanders and leaders can clearly understand and identify to reveal actor agendas or intents. Information collection, with and without unified action partners and along with continuous assessment, supports the commander in developing understanding of unity of effort and unity of purpose. 

###### **_Transformation—Establish Civil Security_** 

7-56. In the transformation phase, HNSF and potentially intergovernmental organization peacekeepers begin to contribute. The BCT focuses more on SFA, particularly on the requisite systems to professionalize HNSF. It continues in partnership with unified action partners IAW the legitimate government binding agreements. Information collection serves to develop further understanding of boundaries, requiring the BCT to shift unit assets and resources to better align with unified action partners and to mitigate sources of instability. The BCT advises and assists the security force leaders, empowering them to assume as much of the security effort as possible. 

7-57. HNSF prominently work on security efforts, so local populations do not perceive the BCT as an invading force to resist. HNSF stay involved to promote their government’s legitimacy and their progress with unified action partners. The BCT assists HNSF information activities, sustainment in support of the HN, protection, and area security operations appropriately. 

7-58. As soon as possible, the BCT transfers HN infrastructure security to HN organizations. HN military units may temporarily be committed to securing public infrastructure, but eventually police forces or dedicated security organizations conduct this function. The BCT continues coordination between unified action partners to help mediate any disagreements among them. 

7-59. The BCT ensures HN forces act with respect to human rights; failure to do so undermines popular support for the HN government and can quickly revert conditions back to those experienced during the initial response phase. Partnered security operations that place HN forces in the lead and those security operations conducted independently of the BCT are the most credible among the civilian population and consequently build the government’s legitimacy through ownership. 

7-60. Initially, the BCT may simply be a support apparatus, or contrastingly, the BCT may make most of the security-related decisions and perform most of the tasks. Nevertheless, HN actors support and increasingly take ownership of such matters. The BCT develops clear MOPs and MOEs that shift security efforts from the BCT to the HN forces in the lead. It also develops indicators of the HN units’ actions and conduct, as well as local public sentiment, that their units can identify while conducting actions in partnership. 

###### **_Sustainability Fostering—Establish Civil Security_** 

7-61. In the sustainability fostering phase, the BCT transitions to a steady state posture focused on advisory duties and SC. The BCT commander implements additional peace measures, depending on further negotiations. During this phase, the BCT enables the HN to sustain the peace. 

###### **Creation of a Safe, Secure, and Stable Environment** 

7-62. BCT forces (which, in this context, are the COIN) seek to create a safe, secure, and stable environment for the local populace. Key to the stability operations task to establish civil security is the development of security institutions or, in their absence, the performance of their normal duties until those capabilities are developed or transitioned to the HN, United Nations, or other U.S. agencies. Commanders and staffs determine the dispositions and compositions of HN armed and intelligence services early in the process. Ultimately, the HN needs to secure its own people. Civil security involves protecting areas, resources, and the populace from both external and internal threats. Ideally, COIN forces focus on the external threats while police and security elements address internal security threats from criminals and small hostile groups. However, during an insurgency, the COIN also addresses the internal security threats from criminals and small hostile groups—notably the armed insurgents. 

###### **_Enforce Cessation of Hostilities, Peace Agreements, and Other Arrangements_** 

7-63. These tasks aid in providing security and stability after an armed conflict while, at the same time, setting the necessary conditions to start disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration. These tasks are critical to providing effective security for the local populace by reducing their exposure to the threat of violent conflict. The tasks help military forces establish a sustained peace by focusing on processes and activities fundamental to conflict transformation. In COIN, most efforts focus on identifying and neutralizing potential adversaries.
