This individual watches body language, and other indicators, for whether the process seems effective. As appropriate, this person can coach more effective techniques to the negotiators or mediators. Leaders also develop a meeting agenda and consider the expected conduct, customs, and actions for the meeting. 

7-153. The third step is communicating. Participants establish an effective means of communicating with all parties. They do not assume a certain leader or element opposes the main effort without careful investigation. Instead, they ensure facts are correct before forming any opinions. The commander earns the trust and confidence of any opposing party. This process includes establishing an atmosphere (and a physical setting) that participants will judge to be both fair and safe.

7-154. The fourth step is executing. Discussion leaders always strive to maintain control of the session; they remain firm, yet evenhanded in their roles. At the same time, they remain flexible and maintain a willingness to accept recommendations from the opposing parties and from assistants and advisors. They settle the easy issues first. They remain prepared to proceed issue by issue in a predetermined order. Actions carry different connotations across cultures. Culture shapes how people reason, what they accept as fact, and what principles they apply to decision making. Also, nonverbal behaviors such as the symbolic rituals or protocols of the arrangement for a meeting are important. If participants cannot reach agreement, they continue dialoguing. At a minimum, they agree on when the parties will meet again. 

7-155. The fifth step is stablishing leader and meeting security. Key leaders and important meetings, even in established, nonviolent, peaceful areas of the world, need security. It allows leaders to focus on the meeting’s purpose without distractions. During a COIN, security becomes an absolute requirement since all key leaders and important meetings are potential targets for insurgents. Successful COIN operations require active public interaction. Such interaction varies from formal meetings and negotiations to informal engagements with local citizens. Formal meetings and negotiations are significant mission events and undergo thorough planning and proper resourcing. Informal engagements happen with little or no planning, but Soldiers still prepare with thorough training and standard operating procedures (SOPs). In most situations, unit leaders, from team leaders up, are the individuals involved in regular interactions and meetings. These personnel are often placed in exposed positions as they execute their missions. At the tactical level, a protective service detail, military police platoon, or squad typically secures a leader, very important person, or meeting. Leaders and units consider several matters when preparing for meetings or negotiations. 

7-156. One consideration when preparing for a meeting or negotiation is for individual Soldier interactions. In a COIN environment, individual Soldiers interact daily with the local populace. While doing so, they maintain situational awareness and remain prepared to react immediately to a range of situations. While one Soldier interacts, another provides security for the first. This is easy under the buddy system. 

7-157. Another consideration is for protective service. At least one person remains ready to provide close, direct, physical protection for the leader. However, the leader’s security does not interfere with the leader’s mission accomplishment, irritate other participants, or include behavior that is perceivable as a threat. During planning, leaders determine any restrictions on people approaching the protected leader and restrict the circulation of people around the leader. If armed at all, the leader carries a sidearm. This choice leaves the leader’s hands free to react to close-in threats. Security personnel take positions from where they can observe everything and everyone near the leader. 

7-158. Finally, a third consideration in meeting preparation is for security. The planning and preparation of crowd control measures occur prior to a meeting, even when crowds are not expected. The planning of evacuation routes and escalation of force procedures for key personnel also occurs. The planning for outer security includes the coverage of inner and outer cordons. In this context, the inner cordon protects the meeting participants, controls access to the meeting, and controls the immediate crowd. The outer cordon isolates and controls access to the meeting. This cordon may be close in and visible or out of sight of the actual meeting, focusing on external elements trying to gain access. 

7-159. Special units or weapons (for example, snipers, shotguns, nonlethal weapons) are employed when available. At least one interpreter, but preferably two, is employed. When two are present, one actively interprets while the other observes body language and listens to side conversations in the audience. All these steps are rehearsed before execution. 

7-160. A typical technique for conducting a meeting is to reconnoiter and conduct a pre-site-clearance of the meeting site (before the meeting). Forces also establish outer and inner cordons, secure the meeting, collapse both cordons, and then conduct an orderly movement back to their base or combat outpost. All these actions should be rehearsed extensively prior to execution. 

##### **PROVIDE SUPPORT TO ECONOMIC AND INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT** 

7-161. By establishing a safe, secure environment, the BCT assists HN actors as they begin the process of achieving sustainable economic development. Other U.S. Government agencies, intergovernmental organizations, and civilian relief agencies often have the best qualifications to lead the efforts to restore and help develop HN economic capabilities. Ultimately, the goal is to establish the conditions in which the HN can generate its own revenues and not rely upon outside aid. The desired end state is a robust, entrepreneurial, and sustainable economy in the HN. All economic development actions build upon and enhance HN economic and management capacities. (See ATP 3-07.5 for information on supporting economic and infrastructure development.) Subtasks in providing support to economic and infrastructure development include those following:

- Supporting economic generation and enterprise creation. 

- Supporting monetary institutions and programs. 

- Supporting national treasury operations. 

- Supporting public sector investment programs. 

- Supporting private sector development. 

- Protecting natural resources and the natural environment. 

- Supporting agricultural development programs. 

- Supporting general infrastructure reconstruction programs. 

- Restoring the transportation infrastructure. 

- Restoring the telecommunications infrastructure. 

###### **Task Organization and Actions to Provide Support to Economic and Infrastructure Development** 

7-162. The BCT’s support toward economic and infrastructure development varies over the range of military operations and AOs. Nevertheless, the efforts toward conflict transformation, unity of effort, and increases in HN government legitimacy, HN ownership, and partner capacity endure through all phases. 

###### **_Initial Response—Provide Support to Economic and Infrastructure Development_** 

7-163. The BCT supports economic and infrastructure development at the local level during the initial response phase by establishing AOs and task-organizing and empowering subordinate units, which it does by allowing them to coordinate with unified action partners. It synchronizes efforts regionally and shifts assets and resources as main efforts change or as opportunities to exploit the initiative arise. The building blocks for broad national recovery and development are set at the local level, and the BCT’s information collection effort focuses on identifying microeconomic information such as changes in commodity or service costs or the number of males without employment and with ages between 15 and 45 years old. Though the BCT maintains responsibility for security, secondary efforts include facilitating the emergence of employment opportunities, infusing monetary resources into the local economy, stimulating market activity, fostering recovery through microeconomics, and supporting the restoration of physical infrastructure to help retain and exploit the initiative. 

7-164. The BCT may have to take the lead in responding to immediate economic needs, including assessing the critical micro- and macroeconomic conditions, during the initial response phase. These economic needs may require HN civilians bringing agricultural products and other goods to safe, secure marketplaces or generating jobs that qualified laborers can fill, for two examples. Unity of effort is essential for the BCT to identify and engage all relevant actors from the HN, U.S. civil agencies, and international organizations. These evolving partnerships and assessments significantly enhance the economic development management transition tasks from the BCT to the U.S. Government civil agencies and HN actors. Hostile individuals and groups can take advantage of gaps when the actors do not engage. They can also exploit opportunities for profit, contributing to long-term instability. 

7-165. Infrastructure reconnaissance is a multi-disciplinary variation of reconnaissance that collects detailed technical information on categories of national or regional public systems, services, and facilities. It informs situational understanding of the local capability to support public infrastructure requirements or of military operations in a specific area. This type of reconnaissance occurs in stages—the infrastructure assessment and the infrastructure survey. (See ATP 3-34.81 for information on infrastructure reconnaissance.) 

7-166. Coordinating with the combat engineer units for an on-site visit, an engineer reconnaissance team can be expected to conduct the initial assessment, with available expertise from the supported unit. The initial assessment provides information to confirm or deny planning assumptions, update running estimates, determine immediate needs, develop priorities, obtain resources, and refine a plan. As operations continue, general engineer and other supporting technical support elements provide qualified teams to perform an infrastructure survey. These teams use the infrastructure assessments from the engineer reconnaissance teams to prioritize categories and identify those parts of the infrastructure to undergo reassessment in more detail. The requisite technical capabilities for performing comprehensive reconnaissance include robust support from joint Service, multiagency, contractor, HN, multinational, and reachback elements.

###### **_Transformation—Provide Support to Economic and Infrastructure Development_** 

7-167. The goal of the transformation phase is to establish a firm foundation for sustainable economic development and to begin to transition control of economic development to U.S. Government civil agencies, international civil agencies, and host-nation (economic) officials and entrepreneurs. The collective emphasis is on establishing HN institutions to provide sustainable economic growth during this phase. Once a civilian administration assumes control, the primary economic development role of the BCT is to advise and assist local leaders. 

###### **_Sustainability Fostering—Provide Support to Economic and Infrastructure Development_** 

7-168. The goal of sustainability fostering sustainability is to institutionalize a long-term, sustainable economic development program and to transition control of the economy completely to HN officials, entrepreneurs, and civil society. This phase also includes steps that build on and reinforce the successes of the initial response and transformation phases. Steps taken during this phase support sustainable economic growth based on a healthy society supported by healthy communities and neighborhoods. The primary economic development role for the BCT is to continue to advise and assist HN civilian economic officials. 

###### **Host Nation Capability and Capacity Development** 

7-169. COIN LOEs to develop HN capability and capacity include both short- and long-term aspects. The short-term aspect concerns immediate problems such as large-scale unemployment and the need to reestablish economy at all levels. The long-term aspect involves stimulating domestic, robust, and broad economic activity. The stability a nation enjoys is often related to its people’s economic situation and its adherence to the rule of law. However, a nation’s economic health also depends on its government’s ability to secure the populace continuously. 

###### **_Support Economic Generation and Enterprise Creation_** 

7-170. Economic recovery begins with an actively engaged labor force. Insurgencies often gain recruits by offering a wage to those without employment. When a tactical unit occupies its AO, its demand on local goods, services, and labor creates employment opportunities for the local populace. Local projects such as restoring public services, rebuilding schools, or clearing roads offer additional opportunities for the local labor pool. Drawing on local goods, services, and labor presents the force with the first opportunity to infuse cash into the local economy, which, in turn, stimulates market activity. However, this initial economic infusion must be translated into consistent capital availability and sustainable jobs programs. Thus, short-term actions are taken with an eye toward enabling financial self-reliance and the creation of a durable enterprise and job market. 

7-171. The local economy requires this stimulus to sustain economic generation and enterprise creation. It includes efforts to execute contracting duties; identify, prioritize, and manage local projects; and implement employment programs. Often, such programs reinforce efforts to establish security and civil order by providing meaningful employment and compensation to the local populace. The assessment of the economic sector includes developing knowledge and understanding of local pay scales; this is essential to establishing jobs programs with appropriate wages. Inflated pay scales may divert critical professionals from their chosen field in pursuit of short-term financial gains from new jobs created by the force. Establishing appropriate pay scales is also significant when the environment includes illicit payment for actions or services in direct conflict with the aims of the force. Adversaries can easily exploit relatively low pay scales and quickly undermine efforts to shape public perception. 

7-172. HN enterprise creation is an essential activity whereby local residents organize themselves to provide valuable goods and services. In doing so, they create jobs for themselves, their families, and neighbors that are inherently sustainable after the departure of other actors. HN enterprises provide various goods and services, including essential services such as small-scale sewerage, water, electricity, transportation, health care, and communications. The availability of financing through banks or microfinance institutions is essential to enterprise creation. Essential tasks may include— 

- Implementing initiatives to provide immediate employment. 

- Creating employment opportunities without age or sex discrimination. 

- Assessing the labor force for critical skill requirements and shortfalls. 

- Assessing the market sector for labor requirements and pay norms. 

- Implementing public works projects. 

- Supporting the establishment of a business registry to register lawful business activity at the local or provincial level. 

- Providing startup capital for small businesses through small-scale enterprise grants. 

- Encouraging the creation of small lending institutions. 

- Enabling the development of financial institutions. 

###### **_Support Public Sector Investment Programs_** 

7-173. Organizations such as the USAID usually manage public sector investment in a fragile state. However, the military force also influences success in these programs. Public sector investment ensures the long-term viability of public education, health care, and mass transit. It also provides for development in resource management and energy industries sourced by mining, oil, natural gas, and hydroelectricity. At the tactical level, units spur investment through grant programs or direct public investment projects. Essential tasks may include— 

- Identifying projects that require large amounts of labor. 

- Prioritizing public investment needs. 

- Developing plans to allocate available resources. 

###### **_Support Private Sector Development_** 

7-174. Developing the private sector typically begins with employing large portions of the labor force. In addition to acquiring goods and services from the local economy, the tasks that support private sector development infuse much-needed cash into local markets and initiate additional public investment and development. Essential tasks may include— 

- Identifying projects that require large amounts of labor. 

- Assessing the depth of the private sector and enterprise creation. 

- Identifying obstacles to private sector development. 

- Facilitating access to markets. 

- Strengthening the private sector through contracting and outsourcing. 

- Providing investors with protection and incentives. 

###### **_Support Agricultural Development Programs_** 

7-175. The agricultural sector is a cornerstone of a viable market economy, providing crops and livestock vital to local markets and international trade. Property disputes, difficulty in accessing nearby markets, poor irrigation, animal disease, minefields, and unexploded explosive ordnance can all hinder its development. Therefore, development agencies prioritize and integrate projects with related tasks in other joint stability functions to establish and institutionalize practical solutions to the long-term growth of the agricultural sector. The military contribution to agricultural development parallels related efforts to spur economic growth in local communities. Together, they draw on local labor pools to help reestablish essential services for the agricultural sector. Essential tasks may include— 

- Assessing the state of the agricultural sector. 

- Encouraging HN enterprise creation to provide goods and services to the agricultural sector. 

- Establishing work programs to support agricultural development. 

- Establishing transportation and distribution networks. 

- Identifying constraints to production. 

- Ensuring open transit and access to local markets. 

- Securing and protecting postharvest storage facilities. 

- Rebuilding small-scale irrigation systems. 

- Protecting water sources. 

- Assessing the health, diversity, and numbers of animals. 

###### **_Restore the Transportation Infrastructure_** 

7-176. Even at the local level, the restoration of the transportation infrastructure is central to economic recovery. An underdeveloped or incapacitated transportation infrastructure limits freedom of movement, trade, social interaction, and development. Goods must reach the markets. Military forces often initiate immediate improvement to the transportation and distribution networks of the HN. These networks enable freedom of maneuver, logistic support, and the movement of personnel and materiel to support ongoing operations. Also, they can reduce the risk of IED attacks on security forces. These improvements facilitate the vital assistance efforts of civilian agencies and organizations that follow in the wake of military forces. Essential tasks during an initial response by military forces may include— 

- Assessing the overall condition of the local transportation infrastructure (for example, airports, roads, bridges, railways, coastal and inland ports, harbors, waterways), including facilities and equipment. 

- Determining and prioritizing essential infrastructure programs and projects. 

- Conducting expedient repairs or building new facilities to facilitate commercial trade. 

###### **_Restore the Telecommunications Infrastructure_** 

7-177. The telecommunications infrastructure exists to support every element of a society, from the government to the financial sectors, and from media to the HN populace. The failure of this infrastructure accelerates the collapse of the HN, isolates the HN government and populace from the outside world, and hampers developmental efforts. Military forces can make only limited contributions to restoration efforts in this area since it contains few essential tasks normally. However, some essential tasks may include— 

- Assessing the overall condition of the national telecommunications infrastructure. 

- Determining and prioritizing essential infrastructure programs and projects. 

###### **_Support General Infrastructure Reconstruction Programs_** 

7-178. General infrastructure reconstruction programs focus on rehabilitating the state’s ability to produce and distribute fossil fuels, generate electrical power, exercise engineering and construction support, and provide municipal and other public services. Such capacity building spurs the rehabilitation efforts that establish a foundation for long-term development. As with restoring essential services, providing support to general infrastructure programs requires a thorough understanding of the civil considerations using the ASCOPE analytical framework. CA personnel support this information collection to help prioritize programs and projects. Essential tasks during an initial response by military forces may include— 

- Assessing the overall condition of the local energy infrastructure. 

- Determining and prioritizing essential infrastructure programs and projects. 

- Assessing the condition of existing power generation and distribution facilities. 

- Assessing the condition of existing natural resources conversion and distribution facilities. 

- Assessing the condition of those existing facilities needed to execute essential tasks in other sectors effectively. 

- Assessing the condition of existing municipal facilities that provide essential services. 

- Conducting expedient repairs or building new facilities to support the local populace. 

###### **_Use Money as an Enabler of Popular Support_** 

7-179. In the long run, it may not be the key enabler to future success, but past experiences have shown using money to secure popular support can assist in furthering the interests and goals of units conducting COIN operations. Money should be used carefully. In most cases, a higher authority tightly controls funds through strict accountability measures that ensure the proper use of the money. With effective use and in support of a desired end state, money can be an effective means for mobilizing popular support for the COIN’s cause and further alienating insurgents from the civilian population. A COIN force can use money to—

- Fund civic cleanup, other sanitation projects, and the equipment to complete those projects. 

- Fund small-scale infrastructure improvements. 

- Fund agricultural projects to improve farming practices and livestock health or to help implement cooperative farming programs. 

- Repair civic and cultural sites and facilities. 

- Repair institutions and infrastructures critical to governance and the rule of law (for example, prisons, courthouses, police stations). 

- Purchase education supplies or repair infrastructures critical to public education. 

- Pay rewards to citizens who provide information on enemy activities and locations. 

- Support the creation, training, and operation of HNSF. 

- Fund events and activities that build relationships with HN officials and citizens. 

- Repair damage resulting from combined and coalition operations. 

- Provide condolence payments to civilians for casualties from combined and coalition operations. 

###### **Development and Reconstruction from the United States Agency for International Development** 

7-180. The BCT staff, ICW division and corps planners, incorporates long-term planning with the U.S. Government, intergovernmental organizations, and NGOs who remain in the country to assist in further development. Incorporating the USAID is essential since it assists in long-term development. Many times, when the U.S. COIN force is involved in reconstruction, the military forces look to make as much impact as possible during their current tour of duty. Commanders ensure military projects and programs do not interfere with the long-range vision of the USAID. History has shown that the necessary duration of involvement to support the transition of organizations exceeds the political will of most external actors. This outcome may be due to financial strains or erroneous expectations about the time requirement. In fact, effective transitions can take decades to complete. In most cases, a post-conflict transition continues long after military involvement. The USAID’s principles of development and reconstruction are useful to tactical units for project selection and small-scale building projects. (See ATP 3-07.5 for additional considerations regarding development and reconstruction from the USAID.) 

###### **Project Selection** 

7-181. COIN units determine and prioritize essential infrastructure programs and projects. The requisite level of effort, the expected duration, the cost, available funding, and the resulting benefit affect priorities. Units help orient various actors, assist them in determining priorities, and assist in monitoring project status. The extent to which the project helps resolve the conflict or contributes to other objectives such as generating employment also affects priorities. Units consult host-nation leaders and other partners regarding such prioritization. Paragraphs 7-182 through 7-190 review the principles guiding project selection and the corresponding use of resources, especially financial resources, in support of COIN operations. 

###### **_Host Nation Ownership_** 

7-182. Units ensure COIN and HN ownership of any project exists. This principle would have the local populace and the government officials who serve them view any project as their own and not one imposed by outside agencies. A locally conceived, funded, and constructed project legitimizes the government and contributes to stability. 

###### **_Capacity Building_** 

7-183. This principle involves the transfer of knowledge, techniques, and skills to local citizens, institutions, and governments, so they develop the requisite abilities to deliver essential services to the population. Ultimately, the local officials and institutions who gain capacity are better prepared to lead their regions through political, economic, and security issues. 

###### **_Sustainability_** 

7-184. By this principle, commanders design and select projects and services most likely to have a lasting effect on the local populace. In other words, the impacts of the projects under consideration would endure after the facility or service is handed off to local authorities and the unit (or contractor) depart from the site. Sustainability implies the local government has the necessary resources to staff and maintain the project. Some commanders have failed to conduct adequate analysis and have built schools or medical clinics only to discover too few teachers or doctors were available to staff these facilities. Other commanders have purchased large generator systems to address electricity shortfalls for neighborhoods in their AOs. However, those commanders failed to address the fuel, maintenance, and service requirements of the systems, so the machines proved an unsustainable solution for the local electrical deficit. 

###### **_Selectivity_** 

7-185. The development community defines this principle as the allocation of resources based on need, local commitment, and foreign policy interests. These strategic characteristics are equally important tactically. Commanders seldom receive all the financial resources they need to implement their essential service, economic, and governance LOEs. Therefore, they must prioritize the allocation of available resources to those reconstruction projects that offer the following advantages: 

- The local government strongly supports them. 

- They will positively impact the most people. 

- They will create the commander’s desired effects. 

###### **_Local Conditions Assessment_** 

7-186. This principle advises the commander and staff to practice care in researching nominations, adopting best practices, and designing for local conditions in their proposed projects. Commanders request or conduct a local conditions assessment before investing financial resources into any potential relief or reconstruction program. Money is not invested in an intelligence vacuum; all available information about local conditions undergoes consideration, such as public requirements, animosities, traditions, capabilities, and economic standings. A detailed assessment of local conditions best advises the commander on a project’s potential to deliver its intended effects. 

###### **_Potential Results Assessment_** 

7-187. This principle relates directly to the principle of assessment and advises commanders to direct resources to achieve clearly defined, measurable, long-term, focused objectives. This development principle is analogous to the military principle of objective, which directs every military operation toward a clearly defined, decisive, and attainable objective. It is equally critical for the commander and staff to assess potential unintended results from their use of money. Many second- or third-order effects from a project may outweigh the benefits from the original intent. 

###### **_Partnership_** 

7-188. This principle encourages close collaboration with local governments, communities, donors, nonprofit organizations, the private sector, international organizations, and universities. Partnership plays a central role in any relief, reconstruction, or development program since it supports each of the other principles of reconstruction and development. In the context of money as a weapon system, effective partnership ensures the unit’s financial resources are well invested and deconflicted with other programs from other agencies. 

###### **_Programmatic Flexibility_** 

7-189. This principle requires units to adapt to changing conditions, to take advantage of opportunities, and to maximize effectiveness as part of their reconstruction and development programs. Just as the conditions for offensive and defensive operations are often changing and uncertain, so are the relief and reconstruction tasks associated with stability operations. These conditions often require commanders to change tactics to achieve their desired objectives. 

###### **_Accountability_** 

7-190. Enforcing accountability, building transparency into systems, and emplacing effective checks and balances to guard against corruption are important components to any relief, reconstruction, or development program. The legitimacy of the commander, unit operations, and local government are reinforced by accountability in all actions, to include the unit’s use of money. 

###### **Small-scale Building Projects** 

7-191. Small-scale building projects encompass almost all construction—both permanent and temporary— that is limited in scale. Examples include schoolhouses, clinics, simple irrigation works, farm-to-market roads, or small police stations. These projects can provide immediate, short-term economic stimuli and long-term benefits to a local area. The HN ideally maintains the highest possible profile and participation in all phases of these projects. Before construction begins, leaders remain aware of the second- and third-order effects of the project, such as which groups will profit from or use the project and any resulting conflicts of interest. They also consider the following: 

- The local populace should need or want the project. 

- The project should support the HN’s plan. 

- The project should support the unit’s COIN mission and long-range plans. 

- The project should support HN civilian authority. 

- The counterinsurgent unit should develop a sustainability plan. 

7-192. Paragraphs 7-193 and 7-194, regarding small-scale building projects, address concept development and project planning. They outline a basic process for conducting each stage. 

###### **_Concept Development_** 

7-193. Concept development identifies needs and potential projects to fill those needs. Soldiers and leaders at every level of responsibility help in identifying potential projects that could serve to further the unit’s and HN’s interests in their AOs. Leaders identify potential projects through meetings with local officials, public interaction, and personal observation of their AOs. Concurrently, possible locations are identified, surveyed, and discussed with the local populace and leaders to ensure suitability. 

###### **_Project Planning_** 

7-194. After site selection, when the project is ready to move forward, the development and implementation of a plan for security occur. The plan incorporates the employment of HN police forces whenever possible. The counterinsurgent unit continually assesses the security situation and adjusts the security plan based on the changing threat. The possibility of sustaining the security forces for the duration of the project receives consideration. Other considerations include those following: 

- Create the design and obtain approval of design. 

- Determine resource requirements such as those following: 

 - Material. 

 - Equipment. 

 - Personnel (professional, skilled, and unskilled labor). 

 - Wages and payment system. 

 - Infrastructure needs (SWEAT-MSO). 

- Conduct available resource assessment of the following: 

 - Local HN civilian resources. 

 - National or regional HN civilian resources. 

 - U.S. civilian and international resources. 

 - U.S. Government and military resources. 

- Determine project participants such as the following and a division of responsibilities across them:  HN national and regional. 

 - Local HN. 

 - U.S Government employees and contractors. 

 - NGOs. 

- Contract the services for the following: 

 - Material support. 

 - Equipment support. 

 - Personnel support (individual labor). 

 - Subcontractor support (specific service). 

 - Infrastructure support (warehouses and sewage, water, electricity, trash, and safety systems). 

- Identify, design, and incorporate information engagement themes and messages. 

- Execute the project and establish periodic progress meetings or reviews. 

- Complete the project and arrange the following: 

 - Ownership handover to HN authorities (preferably local officials). 

 - Follow-up visit (for resolving questions or issues and ensuring sustainability). 

##### **CONDUCT SECURITY COOPERATION** 

7-195. _Security cooperation_ comprises the Department of Defense interactions with foreign security establishments to build relationships that promote specific United States security interests, develop allied and partner military and security capabilities for self-defense and multinational operations, and provide United States forces with peacetime and contingency access to allies and partners (JP 3-20). SC provides the means to build partner capacity and achieve strategic objectives. These objectives include those following: 

- Building defensive and security relationships that promote specific U.S. security interests. 

- Developing capabilities for self-defense and multinational operations. 

- Providing U.S. Forces with peacetime and contingency access to HNs to increase situational understanding of an OE. 

7-196. Army forces support the objectives of the combatant commander’s campaign plan IAW appropriate policies, legal frameworks, and authorities. The plan supports those objectives through SC, specifically those involving SFA (see FM 3-22) and foreign internal defense (FID) (see ATP 3-05.2). _Security force assistance_ comprises the Department of Defense activities that support the development of the capability and capacity of foreign security forces and their supporting institutions (JP 3-20). FID is the participation of the civilian and military agencies of a government in any of the action programs taken by another government or other designated organization to free and protect the populace from subversion, lawlessness, insurgency, terrorism, and other security threats. 

7-197. SFA and FID professionalize and develop security partner capacity to enable synchronized sustainment operations. Army SC interactions enable other interorganizational efforts to build partner capacity. Army forces, including special operations forces, advise, assist, train, and equip partner units to develop unit and individual proficiency in security operations. The institutional army advises and trains partner army activities to build institutional capacity for professional education, force generation, and force sustainment. (See FM 3-22 for information on support to SC.) 

**_Note_ .** SFABs provide SFA to HN FSF. The SFAB provides organic forces to form the basis for the SFAB mission to support FSF. Within the SFAB, the company team is the foundation for the SFAB’s mission and augmented with additional personnel and assets to accomplish the mission. (See ATP 3-96.1 for information on the SFAB.) 

7-198. On occasion, the BCT as a whole or select units of the BCT may support SFA activities, including potentially supporting multiple FSF organizations in or external to the BCT’s AO. Additionally, these FSF organizations may each report through different HN government channels and even to different ministries. To synchronize efforts in this case, U.S. Forces must achieve unity of effort. Similarly, each of the FSF organizational commanders appropriately synchronize efforts with the HN government representatives. (See ATP 3-21.20 for an example of task organization of an Infantry battalion supporting multiple SFA activities, which is useful for discussion purposes.) 

7-199. The stability operations task of conducting SC may have the BCT or one or more select subordinate unit(s), depending on the assigned mission, conducting SFA as a subset of SC. SFA offers a means of support for SC activities in building capacity of an FSF. As soon as the FSF can perform this task, the BCT or selected unit transitions this task within civil security to the HN. 

###### **Initial Response—Conduct Security Cooperation** 

7-200. The initial response phase normally occurs during or immediately after a conflict for which the OE has prevented civilian personnel from operating effectively. The OE is deemed nonpermissive. The objectives of this phase are to improve the security situation, reduce the threat to the civilian population, and create conditions in which civilian personnel can safely operate. SFA in the initial response phase is normally required when FSF lack the capability or capacity to provide the requisite level of security. This phase often requires SFA efforts to help generate, train, or assist new and existing FSF. This phase may require a combination of the types of SFA and considerable support, sustainment, and medical resources. BCT activities during the initial response may be conducted with multinational combat operations to consolidate gains, including providing a safe, secure environment for the local populace. SFA efforts during this phase focus on improving FSF capability and capacity, so all security forces—be they U.S. Forces, other security forces, or FSF—provide a secure environment and reduce the threat. As security conditions improve, transition to the transformation phase begins. 

###### **Transformation—Conduct Security Cooperation** 

7-201. In the transformation phase, SFA activities seek to assist FSF to stabilize the OE in a crisis or in a vulnerable state. The OE in this phase is more permissive than in the initial response phase. However, military forces often need to provide security to some actors. Activities in this phase normally include a broad range of post-conflict reconstruction, stabilization, and capacity-building efforts. The embedded provincial reconstruction team is essential for long-term success. Objectives in this phase include continuing efforts to improve the security situation, reducing the threat to the populace, building HN capacity across the joint stability functions, and facilitating a comprehensive approach toward assisting FSF. 

7-202. The transformation phase entails a broad range of SFA activities to support FSF. The initial response phase differs from the transformation phase in the FSF capability to provide a safe and secure environment. More specifically, FSF may have achieved the level of proficiency at which they no longer need a permanent United States and FSF relationship for tactical operations. However, they may still need full-time advisors and support, sustainment, and medical assistance. Embedded provincial reconstruction team members continue to play a vital role in providing support to governance and developmental efforts throughout this phase. The end state of SFA for this phase sets conditions for the host-nation security sector to provide a secure environment with its own security forces. 

###### **Sustainability Fostering—Conduct Security Cooperation** 

7-203. In this phase, the focus of SFA continues to shift toward assisting the requisite institutions for sustaining FSF. This phase encompasses long-term efforts to assist FSF. They conduct independent operations and can provide a safe, secure internal environment. While this phase may initially require SFA activities, their necessity reduces as FSF become more capable and viable. The policies and conditions of the OE determine the timing of the BCT’s receipt of a change of mission from SFA. Provincial reconstruction teams and other forces may remain to support a theater SC plan. (See section III for details on the BCT’s role in SFA.) 

##### **SECTION II – AREA SECURITY** 

7-204. The BCT engaged in area security operations during COIN is typically organized to emphasize its mobility, lethality, and communications capability. Population-centric area security operations (for example, to consolidate gains) are common across the range of military operations but are almost a fixture during the conduct of stability-focused operations. They typically combine aspects of the area defense and offensive operations (for example, search and attack, cordon and search, raid, ambush) to eliminate the effectiveness of internal defense threats. During the conduct of area security operations, the BCT commander and staff maintain an understanding of the relationship with HN authorities and the civilian population. A clear understanding of the commander’s authority is essential in exercising that necessary degree of control for ensuring security and safety to all military forces and the civilian population located in the BCT’s AO. 

#### **AREA SECURITY OPERATIONS OVERVIEW** 

7-205. Area security operations protect friendly forces, installations, routes, and actions in an AO. During the conduct of stability-focused operations, area security operations establish and maintain the conditions for stability in an unstable area before or during hostilities or for enduring peace and stability after open hostilities cease. They are often an effective method of providing civil security and civil control and supporting SC during stability-focused operations. For example, an area security operation may have to be designed around numerous political constraints. Such a design may align units’ AOs with the HN’s existing political boundaries. Security objectives—regardless of which element of offense, defense, or stability currently dominates—ensure freedom of action over a prolonged period in consonance with the BCT commander’s concept of operations and intent. (See ATP 3-91 for information on area security operations.) 

##### **CIVIL CONSIDERATIONS IN AREA SECURITY OPERATIONS** 

7-206. Civil considerations include the influence of artificial infrastructure, civilian institutions, and attitudes and activities of the civilian leaders, populations, and organizations in the OE on the conduct of military operations. Commanders and staffs analyze civil considerations by the categories of ASCOPE. (See ATP 2-01.3 for information on these categories.) 

7-207. Since civilians are normally present in operations with a dominant stability component, the BCT tends to restrain its use of force when conducting area security operations. However, the commander remains responsible for protecting the force and considers this responsibility when also considering ROE. Everyone receives clear explanation and maintains understanding of the restrictions on conducting operations and using force. Subordinate commanders and leaders and Soldiers remain mindful that their actions, no matter how minor, have far-reaching positive or negative effects. They are aware media (either hostile or neutral) and adversaries can quickly exploit their actions, especially the way they treat the civilian population. 

##### **AREA SECURITY AND LOCAL SECURITY** 

7-208. Area security—a security operation conducted to protect friendly forces, installations, routes, and actions in a specific area—takes advantage of the local security measures performed by all units, regardless of their locations in their AOs. Local security includes any local measure units take against enemy actions. 

7-209. Area security missions inherently require the maintaining of local security. Units use both passive and active measures to provide local security. Passive local security measures include the use of camouflage, movement control, noise and light discipline, operations security (OPSEC), and proper communications procedures. Measures also include employing available sensors, night-vision devices, and daylight sights to maintain surveillance over the area immediately around the unit. Active measures, depending on the situation, include those following: 

- Using observation posts, combat outposts, combat patrols, and reconnaissance and surveillance patrols. 

- Establishing specific levels of alert based on the METT-TC (I) variables. 

- Establishing stand-to times. 

**_Note_ .** Unit SOPs detail activities during the conduct of stand-to. 

7-210. _Local security_ comprises the low-level security activities conducted near a unit to prevent surprise by the enemy (ADP 3-90). All local security activities link to the broader area’s security activities. Local security is closely associated with unit protection efforts. (See ADP 3-37 for information on unit protection efforts.) It includes local measures that prevent or interdict enemy efforts. It is an enduring priority of work, is essential to maintaining initiative, and prevents units from being surprised. It involves avoiding detection and deceiving the enemy about friendly actions, positions, and intentions. It includes finding any enemy forces in the immediate vicinity and knowing as much about their positions and intentions as possible. 

7-211. Local security can be part of the sustaining base or of the area infrastructure. Local security protection ranges from echelon headquarters to reserve and sustainment forces using active and passive measures. Active patrolling, unit SOPs, and continuous reconnaissance are active measures that help provide local security. Passive measures include camouflage use, movement control, noise and light disciplines, proper communication procedures, and ground sensor, night-vision device, and daylight sight use.

##### **ECONOMY-OF-FORCE MISSIONS** 

7-212. The BCT, charged with execution, conducts an area security operation as an economy-of-force mission. Area security missions are numerous, complex, and generally never ending. For this reason, the commander and staff synchronize and integrate security efforts, focusing on protected forces, installations, routes, and actions in the BCT’s AO. Protected forces within the BCT may be subordinate units and elements, echeloned command posts (CPs), and sustainment elements in the BCT’s support area. Protected installations can be part of the sustainment base, or they can constitute part of the area’s civilian infrastructure in a rear area. Protected ground lines of communication include the route network to support the numbers, sizes, and weights of tactical and support area movement in the BCT’s AO. Actions range from securing key points (bridges and defiles) and terrain features (ridgelines and hills) to large civilian population centers and their adjacent areas. 

##### **OFFENSIVE AND DEFENSIVE ACTIVITIES** 

7-213. During the conduct of stability-focused tasks, area security missions are a mixture of offensive and defensive activities involving not only subordinate battalions, companies, and platoons, but also those HNSF over whom the BCT has a command relationship such as operational control or other influence. Offensive area security activities include subordinate tasks of movement to contact (search and attack or cordon and search [see ATP 3-21.20 and ATP 3-21.10] missions) and combat patrols (see ATP 3-21.8), which are designed to ambush detected enemy forces or to conduct raids in the BCT’s AO. Defensive area security activities include establishing base perimeter security (see ATP 3-21.20), establishing combat outposts and observation posts (see ATP 3-21.20), conducting moving and stationary screen and guard missions, and conducting reconnaissance and counterreconnaissance missions (see ATP 3-20.96 and ATP 3-20.97). 

7-214. During offensive or defensive operations, area security activities often serve to ensure the continued conduct of sustainment operations, which support the main and supporting efforts, by generating and maintaining combat power. Area security operations may be the predominant method of protecting those support areas necessary for facilitating the positioning, employment, and protection of the requisite resources for sustaining, enabling, and controlling forces. 

##### **READINESS** 

7-215. During area security operations, forces maintain readiness over longer periods without contact with the enemy. Such periods occur most often when the enemy commander knows enemy forces or insurgents are seriously overmatched in available combat power. In this situation, the enemy commander normally tries to avoid engaging friendly forces unless on terms favorable to the enemy. Favorable terms include the use of mines and booby traps. Area security forces do not develop a false sense of security, even when the enemy appears to have ceased operations in the secured area. The commander assumes the enemy is observing friendly operations and seeking routines, weak points, and lax security to seize an opportunity to strike with minimum risk. Commanders at each echelon influence subordinate small-unit leaders to maintain Soldier vigilance and discipline and thereby to preclude the developments of these opportunities. 

#### **PLANNING CONSIDERATIONS FOR AREA SECURITY** 

7-216. During area security operations planning, the commander apportions combat power and dedicates assets to protection tasks and systems based on an analysis of the OE, the likelihood of threat action, and the relative value of friendly resources and populations. Based on an initial assessment of the OE, the commander task-organizes subordinate units and elements and assigns security areas in the BCT’s AO. Though all resources have value, the METT-TC (I) variables render some resources, assets, or locations more significant for successful mission accomplishment from enemy and friendly perspectives. Throughout the operations process, the commander relies on the RM process and other specific assessment methods to facilitate decision making, issue guidance, and allocate resources (see chapter 4). Criticality, vulnerability, and recuperability are some of the most significant considerations when determining the protection priorities that become the subject of the commander’s guidance and the focus of area security operations. 

##### **AREA SECURITY COMMAND AND CONTROL** 

7-217. During area security operations, the BCT commander devotes considerable time and energy to the problems of coordination and cooperation due to the joint, interagency, and multinational nature of stability-focused tasks. The BCT plans and conducts area security operations in concert with partner participants toward a unified effort, often as a supporting organization rather than the lead organization. The commander employs liaisons to enable unity of effort between partner elements and the coordination centers established by the division or higher commander. 

###### **Interagency and Multinational Organization Involvement** 

7-218. One distinguishing factor of the conduct of stability-focused tasks from the conduct of offensive or defensive tasks is the requirement for interagency coordination at battalion level and below. During area security operations with interagency partners, the commander has inherent responsibilities. These include clarifying the mission; determining the controlling legal and policy authorities; and tasking, organizing, directing, sustaining, and caring for the organizations and individuals for whom the BCT provides the interagency effort. The commander also ensures seamless termination of the mission under conditions in which the identified objectives are met and sustainable after the operation. 

7-219. When operating within or alongside multinational organizations, the BCT commander and subordinate commanders and leaders expect to integrate foreign units down to the company level. SFA activities within an area security mission require carefully selected and properly trained and experienced personnel (as trainers or advisors) who are not only subject matter experts, but also have the cultural understanding, language skills, and seasoned maturity to relate more effectively to and train FSF. Additionally, commanders and subordinate leaders in the brigade support area and battalion trains with the intention to interact routinely with multinational partners during other area security missions. SOPs at subordinate echelons require modifications to incorporate multinational small units who do not have compatible communications and information systems. 

###### **Desired End State** 

7-220. The BCT commander’s definition of the desired end state is a required input to area security operations. While an end state is normally described as a stable, safe, and secure environment during stability-focused operations, this description is insufficient since it does not include the requisite set of conditions for achieving the commander’s objectives. The planning process yields the initial MOEs and MOPs that quantify such an environment. (See chapter 3 for more information.) MOPs and MOEs are important in stability-focused area security operations since traditional combat measures such as territory gained, enemy personnel killed or captured, and enemy combat vehicles destroyed or captured do not apply. The commander ensures the desired end state reflects the prolonged time period associated with many stability-focused area security operations. 

7-221. Achieving the desired end state requires knowledge of operational design (see chapter 4), the ability to achieve unity of effort, and cultural capability (see chapter 1), all related to the BCT’s AO. Through economy of force, the commander identifies a finite amount of available combat power to apply against the essential tasks associated with a given area security operation. Identifying essential tasks lays the foundation for the success of area security operations that seek the future stability of a state. Decisions about combat power use factor in more than the deployed force’s size and relative composition and the mission’s anticipated nature and duration. Assuring long-term stability depends on applying unity of effort to the tasks that are, in fact, essential. 

###### **Information Activities Within Area Security** 

7-222. The final success or failure of the BCT’s area security operation rests with the public perception of those dwelling inside and outside the BCT’s AO and goes beyond defeating the enemy. Earning public trust and confidence is the chief aim of information activities, which integrate and synchronize information-related capabilities to generate effects in the information environment necessary to influence enemy, adversary, neutral, and friendly audiences. 

7-223. Information activities synchronization of information-related capabilities promotes the mission’s legitimacy and reduces bias, ignorance, and confusion by persuading, educating, coordinating, or influencing target audiences. Further, it promotes—through Soldier and leader engagement, CAO, and PSYOP, among other information-related capabilities—audience interaction at all echelons so these target audiences understand the objectives and motives of the BCT and higher HQ. Public interaction also speaks to the scope and duration of area security actions and the broad efforts to build partner capacity (for example, SFA [see section III]). Information activities are essential for achieving decisive results—a stable HN government and peaceful civilian population. 

7-224. The BCT information activities officer or noncommissioned officer (NCO) coordinates with the division (or higher) information activities officer to synchronize information-related capabilities into the BCT’s information activities planning. Synchronization requires the BCT information activities officer (ICW the electromagnetic warfare [EW] office) to participate in targeting within the fire support cell, as well as the various working groups and meetings chaired by the current and future operations and other integrating cells within the BCT. Participation allows for the development of a holistic understanding of the information environment within the problem sets facing the BCT staff. Staff-wide understanding helps synchronize the information activities planning and targeting and allows for shifts in priorities. This synchronization, ICW the information activities and civil-military operations (CMO) managed at the BCT or division level, enables the incorporation of united action partners into planning. 

**_Note_ .** Within the BCT, the information activities officer is responsible for synchronizing and deconflicting information-related capabilities employed in support of BCT operations. The BCT information activities officer synchronizes capabilities within subordinate maneuver battalions and squadrons and within subordinate companies and troops who communicate information to audiences, affect both the content and flow of the information supporting the enemy’s decision making, and protect friendly information flow. The information activities officer prepares appendix 15 and portions of appendixes 12, 13, and 14 to Annex C (Operations) of the OPORD. (See chapter 4 and FM 3-13 for information on the information activities officer.) 

7-225. In the security environment, enemies, adversaries, and other organizations use propaganda and disinformation against friendly efforts to influence various civilian populations inside and outside the BCT’s AO, such as the area of interest (AOI). The BCT’s public affairs staff officer, ICW the division public affairs officer, works closely with the intelligence staff officer to be proactive, rather than reactive, to such attacks. A coordinated information activities plan informs and counters the effects of propaganda and misinformation. The plan (generally developed at the BCT level ICW the division information activities officer and public affairs officer) establishes mechanisms such as a media center or editorial board to educate and inform local and international media—which, in turn, inform the public—with accurate and timely information. Additionally, CAO and PSYOP are integrated into counterpropaganda efforts at the BCT level through the division or higher HQ’s information activities working group. 

7-226. The BCT chaplain can play an important role in bridging gaps with religious leaders and set conditions for future, successful key leader engagements and CAO. During planning, the chaplain advises the commander on matters of religion and culture and on key religious leaders in the AO and AOI. The chaplain and the religious affairs NCO provide important, up-to-date perspectives on local, provincial, and national atmospheres not often included or clear in other sources. They always coordinate efforts with the BCT information activities officer and any BCT information activities working group (see FM 3-13). 

7-227. Without a detailed Soldier and leader engagement plan, different units and staff elements meet with and engage local leaders with different desired end states, thereby undermining the ability of any or all forces to build capacity and to work toward transition to the HN’s leaders. Coordination between staff elements and units within the BCT, when working with the same host-nation representative or office, enables unity of effort and shared understanding of the desired end state for the BCT’s area security operation. A detailed engagement plan identifies differences between provinces or between localities in the province and sets out the objectives to reach the desired end state. Host-nation leaders in a city, district, or province have face-to-face meetings with these leaders to advance HN capacity building. 

7-228. Soldier and leader engagements have significant public impact during all operations occurring among civilian populations. Human beings capture information and form perceptions based on sensory input. We see actions and hear words. We compare physical gestures and facial expressions to the spoken word. The civilian population weighs presented messages from the Soldiers, the leaders of the BCT, and other sources against the conditions surrounding them. When local and national news media are unavailable or unreliable, people turn to alternative sources such as the internet—wherein information flows freely at unimaginable speeds—or rumor and gossip. Perception so often equates to reality. One way to influence perception is to shape information according to how people absorb and interpret information and to mold messages for broad appeal and acceptance. 

7-229. OPSEC is as important during the conduct of stability-focused operations as it is during the conduct of offensive and defensive operations. It contributes to the BCT’s ability to achieve surprise during area security missions, thus enabling the missions’ chances for success. In the BCT’s AO, adversaries and enemies monitor the BCT’s normal activities to detect variations in activity patterns that forecast future operations. They monitor the conversations of Soldiers both on and off duty to gain information and intelligence. Adversaries and enemies monitor commercial internet activity and phone calls from BCT operational and recreational facilities. They search BCT activity garbage. The absence of OPSEC about BCT activities contributes to excessive friendly casualties and mission failures in area security operations just like it does in combat operations. The BCT’s information collection effort hinges in no small part on effective OPSEC. Therefore, measures to protect essential elements of friendly information (EEFIs) are not an afterthought. (See FM 3-13 and ATP 3-13.1 for information on OPSEC.) 

**_Note_ .** The need to maintain transparency of the BCT’s intentions during area security operations is a factor when balancing OPSEC with information release. Commanders and staffs within the BCT maintain knowledge of the release authority for information, including foreign disclosure rules (see ATP 3-16.02). The public affairs and information activities officers (see FM 3-61 and FM 3-13, respectively) lead the coordination and synchronization processes within the BCT. Release authority for information rests with the commander at the appropriate level. 

7-230. Multinational staffs have additional security concerns. Each nation has different access to U.S. Government information systems. Maintaining OPSEC with multinational staff members is difficult, and sometimes, the security rules restrict the ability of multinational partner staff officers to contribute. The chief of staff and foreign disclosure officer at the division level develop work-arounds appropriately (see ATP 3-16.02). One such work-around is to assign a U.S. assistant to the multinational staff officer who will get on a secure U.S. Government information system to ensure the multinational staff officer has the necessary information. The division assistant chief of staff, signal establishes and maintains two separate sets of information systems when this occurs. (See ATP 3-91 and ATP 6-02.75 for information on maintaining OPSEC with multinational staff members.) 

##### **MOVEMENT AND MANEUVER PLANNING** 

7-231. During the conduct of stability-focused operations, the BCT plans its area security movement and maneuver to occur simultaneously with offensive and defensive movement and maneuver, extensively emphasizing security and engagement skills (for example, negotiation, rapport building, cultural competence, critical verbal phrases). Movement and maneuver in the BCT’s AO are normally decentralized to the battalion and company. Through economy of force, the BCT commander determines the right mix of forces to transition quickly between operations as the situation dictates. During area security operations, the commander plans for future movement in the BCT’s AO and in adjacent AOs appropriately. The BCT’s lethal capabilities make possible the execution of area security operations, even with a remote probability of combat. When new requirements develop, the BCT commander plans for any necessary shifting of priorities. 

###### **Fire and Movement** 

7-232. The application of fire and movement lends itself to several offensive and defensive operations (for example, search and attack, cordon and search, area defense) within the civil security and civil control stability operations tasks. Across the range of military operations, the BCT and subordinate units play a major role in ensuring the outcome of stability operations tasks. The BCT and subordinate units are pivotal in the conduct of other stability operations tasks (for example, conducting SC) due to their deterrence value and the flexibility and labor the BCT provides to the division-level or higher commander.

###### **Mobility and Countermobility** 

7-233. Mobility (see chapter 5) and countermobility (see chapter 6) operations are key enablers to area security operations. In stability-focused area security operations, mobility operations allow civilian traffic and commerce to continue or resume. Resuming normal civilian activities in the BCT’s AO is an important objective within stability-focused area security operations. Countermobility operations indirectly support stability-focused area security operations in regard to offensive and defensive operations. 

7-234. Mobility operations focus on keeping ground lines of communication open for both civilian and military activities and reducing the threat of mines and other unexploded explosive ordnances. During area security operations, the commander and staff develop the countermobility plan concurrently with the fire support plan and defensive scheme of maneuver, guided by the commander’s intent. When combat engineer support falls under the mobility and countermobility tasks, it may include those following: 

- Constructing combat roads and trails. 

- Breaching existing obstacles, including minefields. 

- Marking minefields, including minefield fence maintenance. 

- Clearing mines and debris from roads. 

- Conducting route reconnaissance to support the main supply routes and civilian lines of communication. 

- Creating obstacles between opposing factions to prevent easy movement between their positions. 

7-235. The BCT employs roadblocks not only to restrict traffic for security purposes, but also to control the movement of critical cargo. Examples of critical cargo are generators for restoring electrical power in a large area or items that support the general population and resources in the BCT’s AO. 

###### **Area Occupation** 

7-236. Planning for an area occupation or for a relief in place begins before the BCT deploys or, when the BCT is being relieved, redeploys. Planning includes not only BCT forces and their activities, but also other government agencies, multinational partners, HN agencies, and potential international organizations. The METT-TC (I) variables determine the occupation or relief in place that occurs. Sometimes, occupation, much like occupying an initial AO, is appropriate (for example, when the BCT’s stability-focused area security operation occurs with limited intervention or within peace operations). A relief in place may be appropriate during the conduct of an area defense (see chapter 6). However, a stability-focused area security transition by function may be more effective when the relief in place transpires with HN military forces and civil authorities within range of military operations. Some of these functions include medical and engineer services, local security, communications, and sustainment. BCT plans do not remove a provided capability from the AO until the replacement capability is operating. 

###### **Surveillance Systems and Reconnaissance and Security Forces** 

7-237. In restrictive and unrestrictive terrain, the commander relies on crewed and uncrewed surveillance systems and reconnaissance and security forces to collect information in the BCT’s AO. Interrupted line of sight and extreme climate and weather variations often affect the operation of ground and aerial surveillance systems in restrictive terrain. Also in restrictive terrain, reconnaissance and security forces in the BCT’s AO focus on these areas to assist in collection when crewed and uncrewed surveillance capabilities are degraded. A technique for employing reconnaissance and security forces in restrictive terrain that precludes mounted reconnaissance and security forces from covering the assigned area is to use a combat outpost, which is a reinforced observation post capable of conducting limited combat operations. While the METT-TC (I) variables determine the sizes, locations, and number of combat outposts a unit establishes, a reinforced platoon typically occupies a combat outpost. (See chapter 6 and ATP 3-21.10 for information on establishing a combat outpost.) A combat outpost must have sufficient resources to accomplish its designated missions such as conducting aggressive combat patrolling and reconnaissance patrolling. Combat outposts are established when an insurgency threatens the observation posts (see chapter 6 for information on observation post activities) or when enemy forces infiltrating the BCT’s AO might attack the observation posts.

**_Note_ .** During the conduct of defensive operations, the commander uses a combat outpost to extend the depth of the security area, to keep friendly forward observation posts in place until they can observe the enemy’s main body, or to secure friendly forward observation posts that will be encircled by enemy forces. Mounted and dismounted forces can employ combat outposts. 

###### **Army Aviation** 

7-238. Army aviation attack and reconnaissance units with crewed and uncrewed systems—when deployed early with initial response forces—can be a significant deterrent for the domestic combatants, particularly when factions or insurgencies are not yet organized in the initial response phase. Attack and reconnaissance helicopters may be employed to act as a response force against enemy threats. Along with Army aviation attack and reconnaissance (manned and unmanned) and/or organic or tasked echelon-specific unmanned aircraft system (UAS), to include firing, platforms conduct reconnaissance, surveillance, and security over wide areas and provide the BCT with a means for visual route reconnaissance and early warning. Utility helicopters provide an excellent command and control capability to support stability-focused area security operations and to transport patrols or security elements throughout the BCT’s AO. Cargo helicopters provide the capability to move large numbers of military and civilian security force personnel and to conduct resupply when surface transportation is unavailable or when routes become impassable. 

**_Note_ .** BCT plans include measures for the effective use of all resources, including exploiting air power for transportation and resupply over extended distances and, where appropriate, tightly controlled close air support. 

###### **Reserve and Response Force Operations** 

7-239. Maintaining a reserve during any operation is difficult. Often, the commander finds the BCT has more tasks than units to perform them, and stability-focused area security operations are no exception. Nonetheless, contingencies or missions may arise that require establishing a reserve. Maintaining a reserve allows the establishing commander to plan for worst case scenarios, exploit opportunities, provide flexibility, and conserve the force during long-term operations. 

7-240. The response force differs from a reserve in that it is not in support of a particular engagement. It is a dedicated force on a base—with adequate tactical mobility and fire support—designated to defeat Level I and II threats and shape Level III threats until a tactical combat force (TCF) or other available response forces can defeat them. It answers to the establishing headquarters (see ATP 3-91). Considerations when establishing a response force include those following: 

- Threats. 

- Communications equipment and procedures. 

- Alert procedures. 

- Transportation. 

- Training priorities. 

7-241. The commander employs counterfire radars to locate hostile indirect fire systems and thereby to counter an indirect fire threat. Response forces, attack helicopters, or local friendly forces are ideal for responding to counterfire radar acquisitions since clearance of fire procedures are often time consuming and not necessarily reliable at determining locations for HN forces. Additionally, the indiscriminate use of indirect fire on counterfire radar acquisitions can lead to unwanted collateral damage. 

##### **AREA SECURITY INTELLIGENCE** 

7-242. The conduct of stability-focused tasks demands greater attention to civilian considerations—the political, social, economic, and cultural factors in an assigned AO—than does the conduct of conventional offensive and defensive tasks. Using the mission variable of civil considerations and its subordinate categories of ASCOPE, the BCT staff has a standard baseline for analysis to develop understanding. Analyses conducted by organic and attached forces, such as sociocultural analysis, target audience analysis, intelligence analysis, and population and area studies, augment this baseline. During area security operations, the commander expands the IPOE process beyond geographical and force capability considerations. (See ATP 2-01.3 for information on IPOE for stability missions.)

###### **Information Collection for Area Security Intelligence** 

7-243. Information collection, specifically plan requirements and collection assets, enables timely, relevant, accurate, predictive, and tailored intelligence in an AO. (See ATP 2-01 for information on the specific functions for stability missions.) Intelligence cells and knowledge management elements within the BCT and division (or higher) headquarters and battalion and squadron headquarters develop procedures to share collected intelligence data and products, both vertically and horizontally, throughout the force. (See ATP 2-19.4 for information on intelligence techniques for stability missions.) 

###### **Understanding of Potential Threats and of the Populace** 

7-244. Area security operations require the integration of the division and BCT’s information collection effort to develop a clear understanding of all potential threats and the populace. Success in the stability environment requires cultural capability to gauge public reaction inside and outside the BCT’s AO to a particular COA conducted, to avoid misunderstandings, and to improve the effectiveness of the execution of that COA by the BCT or division. Behavioral changes within the general population may suggest the need for changes to tactics, techniques, or procedures or even to strategy. Biographical information, leadership analysis, and methods of operation within the existing cultural matrix are keys to understanding the attitudes of positional civilian leaders and those with referent power toward influencing the outcome of BCT area security operations, either favorably or unfavorably, as well as their capacity for success. 

###### **Indicators of Change** 

7-245. During area security operations, the commander and staff tie PIRs to identifiable indicators of change in the OE, including civilian inhabitants and their cultures, political beliefs, criminal activities, religions, economic classes, and related demographic factors and any variances within affected people-groups. The commander often focuses on named AOIs to answer critical information requirements, to aid in tactical decision making, and to confirm or deny threat intentions, regardless of which element of offense, defense, or stability currently dominates. During area security operations, PIRs related to identifying enemy and adversary activities are tracked appropriately. 

###### **Commander’s Critical Information Requirements** 

7-246. Due to the increased reliance on HUMINT, when conducting area security operations, the commander emphasizes the importance of commander’s critical information requirements (CCIRs) to all personnel within the BCT. CCIRs are information requirements the commander identifies as critical for facilitating timely decision making. Answers to CCIRs come from staff at all levels (see FM 5-0). All personnel receive appropriate guidance to improve the information-gathering capability throughout the BCT. Interpreters speaking to local civilian personnel, security operations, and patrols (combat and reconnaissance) are primary sources of information to assess for economic and health needs, military capabilities, and the political intents of those receiving assistance or who are otherwise a party to the area security operation (see ATP 3-55.4). 

7-247. Planners at the division and BCT ensure any HUMINT assets assigned from outside the BCT are employed effectively, which is typically accomplished by integrating HUMINT collectors at the lowest level possible. The gaining unit accounts for HUMINT asset security and establishes tasking priorities and command relationships for temporary and long-term commitments. (See FM 2-22.3 for information on HUMINT collection.) 

**_Note_ .** Army medical units and elements do not have an intelligence collection mission and ensure strict adherence to the provisions of the Geneva Conventions by avoiding performing such tasks that are inconsistent with their noncombatant status.
